At Lindsay Clancy trial, focus turns to medications prescribed before she killed her 3 children
Lindsay Clancy messaged one of her caregivers less than two months before she killed her three young children in 2023 to say she was having “intrusive thoughts I never had before,” “feeling completely hopeless” and worried about becoming addicted to some medications.
Rebecca Jollotta, a psychiatric nurse practitioner at South Shore Health Perinatal Behavior Health Program, testified at trial Tuesday that she exchanged messages with Clancy regularly on a patient portal throughout in late November and December 2022. Much of their conversations revolved around Clancy reporting trouble sleeping, depressive symptoms and her search for the right mix of medications to treat her symptoms. They also had in-person and virtual visits.
Several times Clancy indicated to Jollotta either that she had not taken the full dose of a prescribed medication or that she wanted to reduce a dosage or change her prescription based on what she felt were intolerable side effects. Clancy also worried about being addicted to some medications like Ativan, but Jollotta said she was not.
___
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.
___
Struggle to find the right medications
“I really don’t like the way I feel on the Remeron and I know that I can’t stick with taking it,” Clancy said in a December message asking to switch from the antidepressant, which also is used to treat anxiety and insomnia, to a previous prescription mix. “I started having very intrusive thoughts that I never had before.”
Jollotta tried to assure Clancy that having intrusive thoughts is common with someone diagnosed with postpartum depression and anxiety and encouraged her to give the Remeron more time to work since she had only been on it a few days.
“This could be some postpartum anxiety. And I wanted to familiarize her with the symptoms, so that she had them written down and she could report them to me,” Jollotta said.
Jollotta, who is among several providers that Lindsay and Patrick Clancy have sued over her care, repeatedly came up with alternative treatment plans for Clancy including suggesting behavior therapy, support groups and meditation. But she acknowledged that it was up to Clancy whether she chose to follow them.
“I’m only making recommendations based on my education experience, training and what I’m seeing in terms of symptoms,” Jollotta said. “The patient has the autonomy.”
During their virtual and in-person visits, Jollotta said, Clancy never talked of having a plan to harm herself or her children. She also never showed signs of psychosis or mania.
But Jollotta acknowledged that Clancy did report having thoughts of suicide. She also suggested that Clancy might have underlying bipolar disorder — due to her days of going without sleep. But Patrick Clancy denied that was the case.
Suicidal thoughts
In mid-December, Jollotta had a call with the couple and was told Clancy had her “worst day” and was “having persistent, intrusive thoughts of suicide.” Jollotta suggested she consider a higher level of care such as that offered by Massachusetts General Hospital. She settled on a Rhode Island program but was soon discharged — with advice to get go one of her antipsychotic medication.
Jollotta, who was going on vacation, said she was concerned that Clancy had been discharged from the hospital, telling her in a message that she could “could benefit from the groups and added support separate even from medication changes.”
She was also concerned that Clancy wanted to go off Seroquel, the antipsychotic medications. Clancy was advised this could lead to “worsening of mood, worsening of sleep,” but she insisted on going off the medication. Jollotta agreed to slowly reduce the dosage.
Killer, or someone who was mentally ill
Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty to murder charges in the deaths of Callan, Dawson and Cora Clancy, who ranged from 8 months to 5 years old. They were found in the basement of the family’s home in coastal Duxbury, Massachusetts, where their mother was lying in the yard. She had jumped from a second-story window, and she remains paralyzed from the waist down.
Prosecutors argue that the former labor and delivery nurse was an intentional killer who contrived to get her husband out of the house and then strangled the children with exercise bands on Jan. 24, 2023. Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham has urged jurors not to view the trial as “a public debate about women’s mental health and how the medical system treats women.”
Clancy’s attorneys do not dispute that she killed the children. But they say she should not be held criminally responsible because she was mentally ill, believing she heard voices ordering her to take their lives and her own.
The defense says she was in the grip of bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis, a rare postpregnancy condition that can alter a woman’s sense of reality. A forensic psychiatrist diagnosed Clancy with those conditions after the killings.

A ferry capsizes on Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba, leaving at least 15 people dead and 27 missing
HARARE, Zimbabwe (AP) — An overloaded ferry capsized on Zimbabwe ‘s Lake Kariba on Tuesday, killing at least 15 people and leaving 27 missing, the national disaster management agency said. It said 77 people were rescued and made it to a small island on the lake, with boats now being dispatched to bring the survivors back.
Zimbabwean state broadcaster ZBC published video of speedboats making their way to what appeared to be an overturned boat on the lake as a helicopter hovered overhead. An underwater team for search and rescue operations was deployed on the huge lake, which forms part of the border between Zimbabwe and neighboring Zambia.
The statement from Zimbabwe’s Civil Protection Unit said it could only confirm through registered ticket sales that there were 114 adult passengers onboard, along with five crew members. There could have been an unknown number of children below ticketing age who were onboard and not accounted for, it said.
The boat has a carrying capacity of 90 people, the agency said, adding its recommendation that the accident be officially declared a disaster.
Mutsa Murombedzi, a local member of Parliament, posted a video of what she said were people on shore waving off what appeared to be the ageing ferry at the start of its journey. She said rural communities use the boat to travel along the lake to the town of Kariba, a journey that usually takes about five hours.
Some people standing on the shore were also concerned if the ferry would survive strong waves on the lake, according to the video.
Earlier, Zimbabwe police had said a rescue operation was underway but did not give any other details.
Kariba is the largest man-made lake in the world by volume and was created in the late 1950s and early 1960s by building a dam wall to block the Zambezi River, resulting in a valley slowly filling with water to form a huge lake that’s now more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) long and up to 40 kilometers (25 miles) wide in places.
Zimbabwe and Zambia share the lake, with the official border between them in the middle of it.

UN says 2 staff arrested by Afghan intelligence agency
Two staff members of the United Nations mission in Afghanistan have been arrested by the country's intelligence agency, the world body told news agency AFP on Tuesday, adding that it had no access to them for two days.
"We confirm that two Afghan UNAMA male staff members were detained by officials of the de facto General Directorate of Intelligence on Sunday, 9 August," in the western province of Herat, the mission said in a statement.
The Afghan government did not immediately comment following the latest claims.
The office of UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called for the staff members' special status to be respected.
"We have not been informed of the charges against them or permitted to see them," Guterres' spokesman Farhan Haq said. "We call on the de facto authorities to ensure compliance with the privileges and immunities of the UN and its officials."
The arrests come just days before the fifth anniversary of the Taliban's return to power, following the capture of Kabul on August 15, 2021.
Multiple UN agencies operate across Afghanistan in a host of areas including health and humanitarian response.
This week, UNAMA published a report in which it recommended the authorities clarify "the rules governing the use of force, arrest, detention" by the security institutions and "strengthen accountability".
The country has been governed for almost five years by the Taliban authorities, which rule according to a strict interpretation of Islamic law.
Afghan women are banned from UN premises, including those who are staff, as well as a host of other places.
About 20 aid workers were arrested in June near the Iran border in Herat province by Afghanistan's morality police, because their beards were not long enough.
They included staff working for organisations that partner with the UN, according to an internal memo reported by AFP, and were subsequently released.
Dozens of women were also detained by the Taliban government's morality police in early June on accusations they were violating official dress codes by not wearing the body-cloaking chador or burqa.
That included a hospital worker employed by Doctors Without Borders (MSF), which strongly condemned the detention.
A rare protest against the restrictions was violently dispersed with at least two people killed, according to the United Nations.
Afghanistan has been hit hard by international aid cuts and faces multiple challenges, including the arrival of millions of its citizens from Iran and Pakistan in recent years.

Belarusian opposition politician and scientist Aliaksandr Milinkevich dies at 79
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:47:22 UTC
05:47:22 KST

The former Sakharov Prize laureate ran against Aliaksandr Lukashenka for the Belarusian presidency in 2006.
Aliaksandr Milinkevich, the physicist-turned-politician who united Belarus’s opposition forces to challenge Aliaksandr Lukashenka in the 2006 presidential election, has died at the age of 79.
His death was announced on Tuesday.
Milinkevich underwent a complicated operation to remove a blood clot from his carotid artery last year. He spent a prolonged period in critical condition and later underwent extensive rehabilitation.
From academia to politics
Milinkevich was born in 1947, in Grodno, Belarus. After graduating from the faculty of physics and mathematics at the Grodno Pedagogical Institute, he worked as a teacher at a local school. He later earned a PhD and became an associate professor at the same institution.
He went on to author dozens of academic works on quantum electronics and laser technology, as well as on Belarusian culture, art, education and more.
Around the time of the Soviet Union's collapse, he moved into the public sector, and from 1990 to 1996, he served as deputy chair of the Grodno city executive committee.
In 2001, he headed the campaign headquarters of Belarusian presidential candidate Semyon Domash, and five years later he ran for the presidency himself.
A pro-European challenger
In 2005, Milinkevich was chosen as the candidate of the opposition democratic forces, which stood as a united front against the Lukashenka regime. A pro-European vision for Belarus became a defining feature of his campaign.
The election campaign was marked by intense pressure on the opposition, including threats of criminal prosecution, disinformation campaigns in pro-government media, and arrests of opposition activists at rallies.
In the end, according to the official figures, Lukashenka took 83% of the vote, with Milinkevich receiving 6%. Both in the United States and in Europe, doubts remained over the reliability of the results and the legitimacy of Lukashenka's third term in office.
That same year, Milinkevich received the European Parliament’s Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought.
After the unprecedentedly harsh suppression of protests in Belarus in 2020, he left the country and lived in exile with his family.
He became an adviser to opposition leader in exile Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya and the founder of the "Free Belarusian University," with its headquarters in Warsaw.
'Return to the European family'
Immediately after the election, Milinkevich founded the civic movement "For Freedom," which he continued to lead for another decade.
The movement championed European values and advocated for the development of civil society in Belarus, free and fair elections, democratic rights and European standards of living.
"By our mentality, traditions, history, culture and language, we are Europeans. For me, it has never been a matter of choosing which way we should go, east or west. For me it has been about returning to the European family from which we were forcibly taken into an empire," he said in one interview.
For Milinkevich, the issue was ultimately existential - "about whether Belarusians will continue to exist in our own country. The master of the Kremlin does not recognise as a nation not only Ukrainians, but us as well," he said.
'A man of exceptional dignity'
Tsikhanouskaya has expressed her condolences to Milinkevich's family.
"A man of exceptional dignity, a kind soul and a brilliant mind, he was a true point of reference for many of us. For me, Aliaksandr was a source of support and wisdom, whose advice I always valued deeply," she wrote in a post on X.
"His devotion to Belarus, our language and culture, and his ability to unite and support people in the most difficult moments will remain with us," she added.
President of the European Parliament Roberta Metsola also responded to the news on social media, writing: "Aliaksandr Milinkevich dedicated his life to the fight for democracy in Belarus."
"His courage and legacy will stay with us. Europe continues to stand with the people of Belarus," Metsola said.
In a 2006 interview, Milinkevich told Euronews: “The humiliation people feel when living in fear, the violation of their dignity — this, I believe, is the root cause of all Belarus’s problems."
For years, he watched as Lukashenka’s regime crushed even the smallest expressions of dissent, stamping out any signs of resistance in Belarusian society. Yet he never lost his optimism. In fact, he said his faith in change had grown stronger after the events of 2020.
"We have experience, we had the fantastic year 2020, when everyone contributed to the Belarusian spirit and the desire to defend their 'self', truth, freedom. After 2020, I am an absolute optimist, because a completely different nation was born. People overcame their fear," he said.

Russia is recruiting women out of prisons to serve as front-line medics. A new investigation documents rape by commanders and criminal cases against the women who report it.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:43:42 UTC
05:43:42 KST

Russia is recruiting women out of prisons to serve as front-line medics. A new investigation documents rape by commanders and criminal cases against the women who report it.
‘You girls are a very powerful destabilizing factor’
In 2024, Russia’s Defense Ministry launched an experiment called “Choice,” according to a new investigation by the independent Russian news outlet Verstka. The military solicited volunteers at women’s penal colonies in several regions and assigned them to tactical medicine units to treat the wounded near the front.
The first group of convicted women was recruited in early 2024 from penal colonies in Russia’s Southern Federal District. “From what I was told, there was no selection process and no training, and the crowd there was… ‘Freedom for AUE’ types [a banned prison subculture that glorifies criminal life]. They were simply told, ‘Want freedom? Sign a contract.’ They thinned out fast. They wiped themselves out: drunken self-inflicted gunshot wounds, a grenade in a dugout, some died from drugs, some were killed out of jealousy… And a small number died carrying out combat missions,” a source told Verstka.
The next round of recruitment took place that fall in Russia’s Irkutsk region, where the women did receive two weeks of training in tactical medicine, taught by former fighters from the Russian mercenary group Wagner. One of the instructors said the women’s commitment was “ferocious.” At the final session, the instructors gave each woman a first-aid kit and advised them never to go anywhere near the front line.
“If women are ending up at war, that’s a sign things are seriously screwed up in the country. If I were a commander and was told women were being brought into my unit, I’d have fought it any way I could. You girls are a very powerful destabilizing factor. Men have been in the trenches for a third year now, and then they bring in women. Hormones will go through the roof, and no law and no army regulation will hold anything together. It’ll turn into chaos,” Verstka quoted one of the instructors as saying. The women did not heed the instructors’ advice, Verstka said.
A source familiar with the women who took the courses said their fates diverged: “Some got a taste of that illusion of freedom and went completely off the rails. Some started building a life for themselves. Some have already died. A small percentage really did try, in good faith, to earn their freedom. I’m talking, above all, about Lyudmila.”
‘You’re a convict, you don’t get that!’
Before her imprisonment, Lyudmila Poltarakova practiced aikido and competed in multi-discipline strength sports. She won the European armlifting championship and earned the Russian rank of International Master of Sports. In 2019, she was convicted on drug charges and sentenced to 15 years in prison after being detained while planting mephedrone dead drops. She pleaded guilty and said she hadn’t used drugs herself but sold them for money to help her brother and sister. After the trial, she was transferred under guard to Penal Colony No. 40 in the Irkutsk region.
One of Poltarakova’s acquaintances described her to Verstka this way: “Very intelligent, prone to calculated risk. She can walk right up to the edge if she’s thought through every move in advance. She doesn’t think like a woman, and she’s extremely strong in spirit, even compared to my comrades in arms. A heightened sense of justice.”
Poltarakova signed a contract, studied hard in the preparatory courses, and arrived in the annexed Luhansk region in early 2025 along with other women from the program. She was assigned to the 370th Medical Battalion and from there sent to the 12th Tank Regiment of the Kantemirovskaya Division, part of the 1st Tank Army, as a medical orderly. The regiment’s commander, Sergei Zhitkov — who goes by the call sign Oskol — began summoning her to his trench, ostensibly for medical massages. The first few times, that was all it amounted to, but later, according to Poltarakova, he began “getting handsy.”
“When he was turned down, he started yelling, asking why the hell her battalion commander had recommended her to him. It turned out that Oskol and [the commander of the 370th Medical Battalion, Ramazan] Mutalipov were old friends, and that it was Mutalipov who had sent Lyudmila to him, saying that she was fine and that he could fuck her,” an acquaintance of Poltarakova said, relaying her account.
Poltarakova later told acquaintances and a military investigator that Zhitkov raped her on February 14, 2025, and continued to do so for at least the whole of March. Many of their fellow soldiers witnessed the assaults, she said. “The whole 12th Regiment was talking about it. And when Oskol called our dugout one night in April and told us to go provide sexual services to the division commander, who had come to visit him, I couldn’t take it anymore. I started screaming, I had a breakdown,” Poltarakova said in a voice message to a friend.
Other medics who shared a dugout with Poltarakova witnessed the scene, as did the military police officers guarding it. According to Poltarakova, another woman was sent to Zhitkov that night, while she herself was sent back to the 370th Medical Battalion. Poltarakova signed a statement saying she had no complaints against Zhitkov. She did so voluntarily, fearing that publicity would “negatively affect her future service and her receipt of an award to expunge her conviction,” according to her testimony, which Verstka reviewed.
In June 2026, Poltarakova was wounded and ended up in a military hospital, where, she said, she began getting threatening phone calls demanding that she sign another statement saying she had no complaints against Zhitkov. She then filed a rape complaint with the deputy military prosecutor of the 1st Tank Army and made her story public on a pro-war Telegram channel.
“I can say that we’re all slaves with no rights. You want a medal for being wounded? You’re a convict, you don’t get that! They struck me off the list for a medal! … You want leave after eight months of hellish work on the front line? You’re a convict, you don’t get that! You just want to rest in the hospital after surviving at the front? You’re a convict, you don’t get that! No one has ever thrown my criminal record in my face this often! I’ve served honestly since the first days of my contract; I don’t hide in hospitals, I’m always on the front line. … They never humiliated me in the penal colony the way they have in the army,” she said in a video statement.
After filing the complaint, Poltarakova was told she was being sent on a combat mission — an order she refused, believing it was an attempt to get rid of her. She dropped out of contact on July 15, but not before telling acquaintances that military police had come for her at the hospital. Verstka later learned that Poltarakova was alive and on the front line. A criminal case has been opened against her for refusing the order to leave the hospital for a combat mission. No case has been opened over the rape. Zhitkov was promoted in 2025 to acting commander of the Kantemirovskaya Division.
‘A guy comes up to me and says he’ll throw a grenade into my dugout if I don’t put out’
Darya Chirukhina dropped out of contact at the same time as Poltarakova. Another former convict from the Irkutsk region, she had also been assigned to the 370th Medical Battalion and had spoken publicly about attempted sexual assault.
“I’m posted at an outpost where some guy comes up to me and says that he’s the brother of an FSB [Federal Security Service] officer and that he’ll throw a grenade into my dugout if I don’t put out. She also complained about the workload and health problems: “Even in the penal colony, I had more rights when it came to dealing with my own affairs… I developed diabetes at the front. I asked the command for medical help again and again, and for six months they just turned me away. Our commanders used manipulation and pressure to make me file a formal refusal of treatment. When the top brass come to visit, they hide us on purpose so we don’t say anything we shouldn’t…”
Other women from the penal colonies who spoke with Verstka also described consensual relationships at the front that resulted in children. “Things get truly awful when it comes to the kids — the babies aren’t even a month old, and they take them away from the mothers. I sent the babies away [from military hospitals] myself, and I still feel sick about it,” one of the convicted women said.
Verstka’s sources among former inmates said they knew of at least three births at the front. The women who gave birth were threatened with having their children sent to an orphanage, but in the end managed to hand the infants over to distant relatives. They then continued to serve “under compulsion,” the sources claimed.

In Gaza’s tents, widows face war’s harshest realities alone
Widows in Gaza struggle alone under displacement, burdened by loss, insecurity, and daily battles for survival.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Under the scorching heat inside a displacement tent in northern Gaza, Mona al-Masri tries to plan for each day as it comes.
Mona is a widow, and the mother of four children, ranging in age from nine to two. Her husband, Mohammed, was killed in an Israeli strike in September 2024.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran, US set new conditions during Hormuz talks: What does this mean?
- list 2 of 3Palestine weekly: Netanyahu hedges on Gaza roadmap
- list 3 of 3Colombia’s far-right government recognises Israeli claim over Golan Heights
Between fabric walls that provide little protection, Mona carries the responsibilities of a family burdened by displacement brought on by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and the accompanying loss of security.
Mona begins each morning trying to secure her family’s basic needs, searching for water, arranging food, and attempting to protect her children from a reality that no longer resembles the life they knew before the war began in 2023. She says that what hurts her most is not only the harshness of their living conditions, but also the feeling that she has been forced to confront every detail of daily life alone.
“There is no normal life inside the tent. Every day begins with the same questions: how will we secure our needs, and how will we get through another day surrounded by this exhaustion?” Mona says. “The war did not only take away our homes; it took away our sense of safety and stability and made even the simplest things require enormous effort.”
Rising numbers
Mona is one of thousands of women in the Gaza Strip who have found themselves facing new roles imposed by the war, taking care of their families by themselves.
According to data from the Ministry of Social Development in Gaza, the total number of widows in the Gaza Strip has risen to more than 50,000. The figure includes 28,224 women who became widows as a result of the war, in addition to more than 22,500 widows who were already registered with the ministry before the war.
Aziza al-Kahlout, spokesperson for the Ministry of Social Development in Gaza, says the number is expected to rise further because not all widows have yet been registered.
“The war has left these women facing a difficult reality, including the responsibility of supporting their families without a provider, amid widespread destruction and the collapse of the basic conditions needed for a decent life,” al-Kahlout says.
“This requires effective programmes for economic empowerment, job creation and strengthening self-reliance to help lift them out of poverty and deprivation,” she says.
Al-Kahlout stresses that widows’ needs extend beyond financial assistance. They also require psychological and social support, healthcare, and legal assistance related to guardianship, custody, financial rights and inheritance.
“Protecting and empowering widows in the Gaza Strip has become a shared national and humanitarian responsibility that requires an urgent and sustainable response,” al-Kahlout says.
She explains that widows need regular financial assistance, emergency relief, psychosocial and healthcare services, legal support and educational opportunities, in addition to vocational training and support for small and family businesses.
Psychological support
The loss of a husband during the war has not only deprived thousands of women of their life partners, but has also been accompanied by displacement, the destruction of homes, and the loss of stability.
Aseel Abu Shaweesh, a psychologist, explains that losing a husband during war represents a traumatic experience with profound psychological and social impacts on widows and their children. She notes that many women who lost their husbands have found themselves facing new and increasing responsibilities while simultaneously dealing with their other troubles.
“A widow in Gaza faces the pain of losing her husband, the responsibility of supporting her family, and caring for her children in an environment filled with fear and instability,” Abu Shaweesh says.
She adds: “Many women are forced to hide their grief and emotional collapse so they can carry on in front of their children, while the accumulation of daily pressures and the lack of space to express their pain increase levels of anxiety and psychological exhaustion.”
Abu Shaweesh explains that children in families who have lost one parent are also deeply affected, especially when the loss of the father is accompanied by displacement and deteriorating living conditions.
“A child loses their father and their sense of safety and stability. They may show signs of constant fear, sleep disturbances, and behavioural changes as a result of the difficult experiences they have endured,” Abu Shaweesh says.
The psychologist emphasises that widows’ needs include financial assistance as well as psychological and social support services to help them adapt to the new roles imposed by the war.
“These women need continuous support that helps them regain a sense of safety and the ability to manage their lives and their families under these difficult circumstances,” she says.

Fishermen face deadly dangers as Yemen’s Red Sea becomes a warzone

Fishermen face deadly dangers as Yemen’s Red Sea becomes a warzone
Many Yemeni fishermen have abandoned the trade, seeking safer livelihoods as Red Sea becomes too dangerous.
Al-Makha, Yemen – Mazhar works on a sea that has long been a front line in Yemen’s conflict.
The fisherman, based in the city of al-Makha (also known as Mocha) on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, has long struggled to make a living since war arrived in the region in 2015.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump demands compensation from Iran as talks on Strait of Hormuz continue
- list 2 of 3Iran, US set new conditions during Hormuz talks: What does this mean?
- list 3 of 3Yemen’s Houthis launch ballistic missile attacks on al-Makha and Marib
Fuel is expensive, and so is renting a boat. But Mazhar, who is in his 40s and has a family that solely relies on the income from his fishing, has a bigger problem: whenever he sets out for the sea, he might not return home.
“Recently, a fishing boat in al-Khawkhah was fired on, and we lost two colleagues,” Mazhar said. “No one knows why, and the authorities haven’t announced the cause of the incident.”
Venturing beyond the shoreline is a dangerous gamble since the sea turned into a battlefield – Mazhar knows fishermen who have gone missing without a trace. But when there’s no food left at home, he decides to risk it anyway.
Red Sea restrictions
Yemen’s Red Sea coast is one of the main hubs of the country’s fishing industry, which before the war was the country’s second-largest source of export earnings after oil.
The Red Sea fishing industry has been impacted since the early years of the war, with fish exports from the region falling by about 70 percent, according to a 2018 study.
The region is strategically important for other reasons, too. Yemen’s principal port of Hodeidah sits about 160 kilometres (100 miles) up the coast from al-Makha, and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait lies at its southern entrance, controlling entry into one of the world’s most vital waterways. All of that means that the coastline has been heavily contested since the early days of the war.
Currently, the Houthi rebels control most of the territory from Yemen’s border with Saudi Arabia down to Hodeidah, with pro-government forces, largely the Guardians of the Republic force, operating south of the port city. The front line had been quiet in recent years, but recent Houthi attacks against pro-government forces across the country have also targeted al-Makha.
But it is events in the waters of the Red Sea that have drawn the most attention internationally. The Houthis began regularly striking shipping passing through the region after the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, and have also recently attacked Saudi shipping. The attacks have prompted the United States, the United Kingdom, Israel and Saudi Arabia to strike Houthi targets in Yemen at various times, including on the Red Sea.
Mazhar explained that fishermen now face strict boundaries at sea that they cannot cross. That is not only the case in al-Makha, but also in neighbouring al-Khawkhah district and large parts of the entire Red Sea coast.
“We pay money to buy scrap barrels and car bodies to dump into the sea to form artificial reefs. However, with every escalation in the Red Sea, we are denied access to our reefs for military reasons and are forced to fish near the shore,” Mazhar said.
Threats
“I cannot name the party restricting us right now because I am a fisherman, and speaking out could put me at risk,” Mazhar said. “But both warring sides have prevented us from sailing at different times. We are the victims of every faction fighting in our area.”
Before 2018, local fishermen say that the National Resistance Force (which the Guardians of the Republic forces later emerged out of) prevented fishermen from venturing into deep waters and reaching their reefs. Although restrictions were later eased, the fishermen say that both the Houthis and pro-government forces have placed restrictions on sailing since 2023.
“In the end, it is the fishermen who suffer to provide for their families,” Mazhar said. “We have no hand in this war, yet we bear its worst consequences.”
He added that several of his fellow fishermen have been arrested after being accused of smuggling or aiding one faction against another – claims he says are completely unfounded.
Akram, who also works as a fisherman in al-Makha, describes another danger: sea mines.
“Last year, I left home alongside two of my neighbours, and a sea mine exploded under their boat near the shore in al-Khawkhah,” he recalled. “It’s a sea mine; how can we avoid it? I can say with certainty that the Red Sea is no longer safe, and we have to move elsewhere.”
“We are witnessing the worst days in the Red Sea,” Akram added. “To be a fisherman in the Red Sea, you must carry your shroud on your shoulders.”
Fouad Doubla, head of the Fishermen’s Association in al-Khawkhah, told Al Jazeera that more than 30,000 fishermen have been affected by the conditions on the Red Sea coast and are struggling to provide basic necessities for their families, as fishing is their sole source of income.
Doubla noted that 113 fishermen have gone missing in the Red Sea since 2023, with their families receiving no information about their whereabouts. He added that the presence of sea mines is a direct consequence of the war that continuously threatens fishermen’s lives.
“Sea mines have killed 264 fishermen and maimed 215 others, forcing many to stop fishing and look for alternative work,” Doubla said, adding fishermen had also been detained by pirates in the Red Sea.
Alternative choices
Doubla explained that the difficulties and dangers encountered by fishermen have many looking for a different way to make money.
“When fishermen realised they could no longer sail safely and that their families lacked food, they were left with no choice but to either risk their lives at sea or find another job – and many chose the latter to stay safe,” Doubla said.
For Akram, that means relocating to Aden, where he believes fishing on Yemen’s southern coastline will be safer.
“Nothing is worth risking our lives for. The families of those who were lost are now struggling just to find enough food. I encourage my colleagues to join me and move to a safe area.”
Ismail, a 48-year-old who comes from a long line of fishermen, decided to leave the profession behind entirely last year, selling the gear he had collected over 20 years and using the proceeds to buy a minibus instead.
“Danger surrounds fishermen from every direction, and we never know when we will meet our fate at sea,” Ismail told Al Jazeera while holding the steering wheel of his minibus. “I don’t think any wise man would continue fishing amid such danger.”
Ismail’s wife supported his decision to quit fishing and sold some of her jewellery to help him start his new business, relieved to end the constant anxiety she and their five children felt whenever he went out to sea.
“Sometimes we stayed at sea for four days, which was completely normal under regular circumstances,” Ismail said. “But nowadays, it isn’t safe. When I stayed out for more than a day, my family would panic, and I think they had every right to be worried.”
Today, Ismail earns a modest income driving his minibus, but he is content knowing he is safe and able to share every meal with his family without constant fear.
Mazhar, who continues to fish close to their shore, believes those who transitioned to new jobs have made the right choice.
“I’ve thought more than once about leaving this dangerous profession, but I have no alternative,” he said. “As soon as I find one, I won’t hesitate for a second.”

The Perseids will peak in Ukraine tonight – when and where to watch the meteor shower
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

The Perseids will peak in Ukraine tonight – when and where to watch the meteor shower
Kyiv • UNN
The Perseid meteor shower will peak on the night of August 13, coinciding with the new moon. The best time to observe it is after midnight, far from city lights.
The Perseid meteor shower will peak on the night of August 12–13, and this year it will be especially visible in Ukraine because of the new moon, which will not brighten the sky. NBC News and astronomical resources report this, UNN writes.
Details
The Perseids can be observed every year from approximately mid-July to the end of August, when Earth passes through the stream of debris from comet 109P/Swift–Tuttle. Dust particles and other material enter the atmosphere at high speed and burn up, creating bright streaks known as "shooting stars." The peak of activity in 2026 will occur on the night of August 12–13.
This year, the viewing conditions will be more favorable than usual. The Perseid peak coincides with the new moon, so bright moonlight will not interfere with seeing fainter meteors. Under dark skies and favorable weather conditions, dozens of meteors per hour may be visible, and under ideal conditions, their number may approach 100.
In Ukraine, the best time to observe the Perseids is after midnight, when the meteor shower becomes more active. The greatest chances of seeing shooting stars will be during the second half of the night—closer to dawn. No telescope or binoculars are needed for observation: it is better to look with the naked eye in order to take in as large an area of the sky as possible.
How to See the Perseids in Ukraine
For observation, it is worth traveling as far as possible from cities, street lighting, and other sources of light pollution. An open location with a wide view of the sky is best. Before observing, it is advisable to give your eyes at least 15–20 minutes to adapt to the darkness and avoid using a bright smartphone screen.
Leonid's unique starfall: when Ukrainians will see the celestial show14.11.24, 05:24 • 99491 view
It is not necessary to look directly at the constellation Perseus. The shower's radiant—the point from which the meteors appear to fly out—is located there, but individual flashes may appear across a significant portion of the sky. Therefore, the best strategy is to lie down or sit so that you can see as large an area of the sky as possible and observe for an extended period.
On August 12, Ukraine will also fall within the visibility zone of a partial solar eclipse. In Kyiv, it will begin at approximately 20:14, reach its maximum at around 20:18, and end at about 20:23 Kyiv time. The eclipse will not reach totality in Ukraine.
After the eclipse ends, you can wait for darkness and then turn to observing the Perseids. The meteor shower will remain active after the peak, but the night of August 12–13 is considered the best time to observe it in 2026.

Romanian military destroys 2 Gerbera drones found in Black Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:23:25 UTC
05:23:25 KST

Romanian military divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones found drifting near an offshore gas project in the country's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta said on Aug. 11.
The drones were discovered about 90 nautical miles off the coast of Constanta near the Neptun Deep offshore gas project by a civilian vessel conducting work in the area, Miruta said in a social media post.
A Romanian Coast Guard vessel was dispatched to the area, where authorities identified two drifting drones and additional debris.
Explosive ordnance disposal divers from the Romanian military subsequently destroyed the two Gerbera drones through a controlled detonation to ensure the safety of the waterway and ongoing operations around the platform.
Romanian authorities contacted Ukraine following the discovery. "We contacted our Ukrainian partners, who confirmed that the systems do not belong to them," Miruta wrote.
He did not say who was believed to have operated the drones or how they reached the area.
The Gerbera is a Russian-made multipurpose drone modeled on the Iranian-designed Shahed-136. Russian forces first deployed Gerbera drones against Ukraine in 2024 and have used them for strikes, reconnaissance, and signal relay.
Romania's exclusive economic zone covers roughly 22,485 square kilometers (8,681 square miles) of the Black Sea, extending beyond the country's territorial waters, which reach 12 nautical miles from its coast. The maritime boundary between Romania and Ukraine was established in 2009 following a ruling by the International Court of Justice.
Romania, a NATO member, also shares a roughly 614-kilometer (382-mile) land border with Ukraine and has repeatedly reported Russian drones or drone debris entering its territory during attacks on neighboring Ukraine.
Most recently, Romania scrambled two F-16 fighter jets on Aug. 2 after detecting a drone near its border with Ukraine during a Russian attack on southern Ukraine. The drone entered Romanian airspace for about 20 minutes before returning to Ukraine, where Romanian authorities said it was shot down by Ukrainian forces.
The Black Sea has also faced other security threats since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, including drifting sea mines that have threatened shipping along key trade and energy routes.

LONDON, August 11. /TASS/. The United Kingdom is interested in resuming contacts with the Russian top brass to avoid incidents that may trigger a direct military confrontation between the two states, The Times wrote.
According to the report, UK military chiefs fear an "unintended escalation" caused by the lack of dialogue with Moscow. The question of reopening channels of military communication was raised after Russia’s Admiral Grigorovich frigate had to fire warning shots in the English Channel during an unsafe approach by a UK-flagged yacht.
Chief of the Russian General Staff Valery Gerasimov last spoke to chief of the UK defense staff Adm. Tony Radakin in September 2022. The latest reported conversation between the defense ministers of the two countries occurred in October 2022, when Defense Minister Sergey Shoigu phoned his UK counterpart Ben Wallace to express his concerns about the possibility of provocative acts on the part of Ukraine with the use of a dirty bomb. Attempts to resume dialogue have been unsuccessful since.
A spokesperson for the UK government confirmed London’s intention to restart military communication channels with Moscow.
"Our Embassy in Moscow enables us to deliver clear and robust messages directly to the Russian Government, helping to protect UK interests and manage risks of escalation," she said.
Expulsion of attaches
According to The Times, normally negotiations between top military officials are organized by military attaches, but the UK expelled Russia’s envoy in 2024, claiming that he was an "undeclared military intelligence officer." Moscow took reciprocal measures.
Former UK military attache in Russia and Ukraine John Foreman described London’s decision as counter-productive and urged the UK authorities to resume ties with Russia.
"A major misunderstanding could ultimately lead to people dying," he said. "You need to talk face to face to get any traction with the Russians."
In his view, "talking clearly and directly with your adversary in private isn’t weakness."
According to the newspaper, the hotline between the two nations still exists, but it is not being used as often as was before the start of the special military operation in Ukraine. According to Foreman, this line alone is not enough to avert miscalculations.

Ultra rare Nintendo Mario game cartridges discovered in Wisconsin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:23:02 UTC
05:23:02 KST

Ultra rare Nintendo Mario game cartridges discovered in Wisconsin
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A few years ago, a pop culture store owner in Wisconsin mentioned to Jason Ganos, a well-known Nintendo game collector, that he had a box of Super Mario cartridges that had been sitting in storage for years. It stopped Ganos in his tracks.
It turned out to be an ultra rare collection of 97 “absolutely pristine” copies of Super Mario Brothers Duck Hunt, a popular Nintendo game that had been released in 1988, Ganos said.
After some initial research, Ganos found that the cartridges he held were not only a new variant of the game, but also the last known production date of it.
Most of the cartridges will go up for sale Friday in an online auction that will run until Sept. 9.
“I still don’t quite believe that any of this is happening,” Ganos said. “I just think it’s kind of serendipitous that this happened. It’s just still very bizarre to me.”
Ganos, a hard-core fan covered in Nintendo tattoos and who has operated Nintendo Wire, a news service for Nintendo announcements and nostalgia for over 10 years, said he would not venture to guess how much the games are worth.
But when he saw the box, he immediately knew it was special.
“It’s like pulling out like a Holy Grail,” Ganos said, later adding, “they’re gorgeous.”
The discovery came after the owner, Kevin Braun, of One Stop Wonders in Waukesha, outside Milwaukee, asked Ganos to help him sell some stuff, including common Nintendo games and Pokémon cards.
Braun mentioned the box of Mario cartridges that had been sitting in storage for years. He recalled buying them from a customer whose family had kept them for metal scraps but thought they were not worth much.
The cartridges of Super Mario Brothers Duck Hunt he had were made in 1993, long after the company discontinued the bundle in 1991. Braun and Ganos still aren’t sure why the copies they possess were made but assume they were either warranty replacements or part of a bundle with a box retailer that never panned out.
Knowing the potential significance of the possession, Ganos booked a flight immediately.
“I flew down to California with 97 carts in my carry-on luggage, sweating bullets going through TSA, like why do you have 97 little circuit boards in your carry-on?” Ganos recalled thinking nervously.
He anxiously made it through airport security to meet with video game experts to have the cartridges verified and graded, giving them a perceived value.
There had never been a cartridge rated a perfect 10, on a .01 scaling basis at Professional Sports Authenticator video games, Ganos said.
Five of the 97 Ganos possessed received a perfect score.
“I think there’s going to be historic significance to the tens,” Ganos said when talking about how much the games may sell at the auction. “Like number one, it’s so many people’s childhoods, and number two, there’s never been a 10 in an NES cart before.”
Ultra rare video game cartridges, especially ones with unique production history, can be sold for six- to seven-figure prices in the collector’s market. Ganos said the 97 carts are also unique because of their perfect condition, which, much like comic books or sports cards, often makes them sell for higher prices.
Ganos can’t estimate the ultimate worth of the cartridges because they are incomparable to other video game collectibles he has seen before. They could be worth hundreds, thousands or tens of thousands, he said.
Ganos and Braun are only auctioning off three of the perfect 10 scored cartridges at Golden Pop’s Culture Auction beginning Friday. They are both keeping one copy with a score of a 10, and a few others rated in the higher 9’s.
The games can be played if the buyer wants. But because they are pristine, Ganos hopes to keep them that way.
“Finding uncirculated stuff for me is just like super exciting,” Ganos said. “This game was the first video game I’ve ever played. Mario Duck Hunt was just such a big part of my life growing up.”
Braun and Ganos also plan to do a charity auction after they are finished with the current one.

Seven Employees Killed, Dozens Injured in Russian Strike on Metinvest Plant in Zaporizhzhia

- Category

Seven Employees Killed, Dozens Injured in Russian Strike on Metinvest Plant in Zaporizhzhia
A Russian ballistic missile strike overnight targeted the Metinvest industrial site in Zaporizhzhia, killing seven employees and injuring 21 others, Metinvest Group Press Office reported on August 11.
This strike was a part of a massive bombardment across Ukraine, in which Russia launched Zircon anti-ship missiles, Iskander-M and North Korean KN-23 ballistic weapons, alongside 120 attack drones. While the strikes wrought severe devastation and multiple civilian casualties in Zaporizhzhia, the Kyiv region was also heavily targeted. Missile impacts ignited commercial warehouses and struck the grounds of a children’s hospital.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The attack struck as workers were heading to emergency shelters immediately following an air-raid alert. The company expressed its condolences, stating that the loss of the seven Zaporizhstal team members is a massive blow to their families and loved ones.
The 21 injured colleagues are currently receiving all necessary medical assistance, and the company remains in contact with the families of the victims to provide support during this incredibly difficult time, the press service reported.
“The civilian industrial facilities in Zaporizhzhia, which provide jobs for tens of thousands of people and produce vital metallurgical and coke-chemical products, sustained severe damage in the strike,” the company wrote.
The Russian attack heavily damaged energy units, general plant infrastructure, and the main and auxiliary capacities of the coke and blast furnace production lines.
As a result, operations at the primary metallurgical combine have been completely suspended, while other associated production sites have been forced to operate at reduced capacity, according to the company.
Specialists are currently on-site assessing the full extent of the destruction, evaluating the possibilities and timelines for recovery, and conducting necessary emergency repair work. Metinvest extended its gratitude to the plant’s internal services, emergency responders, and city services involved in mitigating the aftermath and assisting the victims.
In mourning for the deceased employees, flags across Metinvest enterprises in Zaporizhzhia have been lowered to half-mast today and tomorrow, the press office stated.
The attack on the industrial plant followed a heavy bombardment of the city just one day prior. On August 10, Russian forces struck Zaporizhzhia with guided aerial bombs (KABs), injuring at least 24 civilians—including a 10-year-old girl who was hospitalized in serious condition.
The daytime strike damaged a five-story residential building, ignited multiple fires, and cut power to roughly 7,500 residents, prompting the regional prosecutor’s office to open a war crimes investigation into the attack.

Russia frees ex-US Marine Robert Gilman after family warned he was ‘on the verge of death’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:20:35 UTC
05:20:35 KST

Russia released former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman from prison on Tuesday after more than four years in custody, just days after his family warned that his health had deteriorated so severely that he could be close to death.
U.S. officials told Reuters that Gilman, 32, who was jailed in Russia in 2022 after authorities accused him of assaulting a police officer while intoxicated, was pardoned by President Vladimir Putin on humanitarian grounds.
Past releases of detained Americans from Russia have often taken place as part of prisoner swaps. President Donald Trump, however, said Moscow had asked for nothing in return and that no Russian prisoner had been released in exchange for Gilman.
Trump posted a photo on Truth Social showing Gilman aboard a plane bound for the United States, looking extremely thin and sitting alongside his mother, Nancy, as others on the flight held up an American flag.
“I am proud to announce that American Citizen Robert Gilman, a former United States Marine, is coming HOME!” Trump wrote.
“In a well known Media story, Robert was imprisoned in Russia in 2022, during the Biden Administration. After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis.”
Trump said Moscow had not sought anything in return for Gilman’s release.
“We appreciate this decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange took place,” he wrote.
Trump said Gilman was expected to land later Tuesday at Andrews Air Force Base in Washington, D.C., where administration representatives would meet him.
“I just spoke to him, and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands. I will take care of that!” Trump wrote.
He added that Gilman had been reunited with his mother, Nancy, who was traveling with him on the flight home, and thanked members of his team involved in securing the release, including Steve Witkoff, Adam Boehler, Sebastian Gorka and Jared Kushner.
U.S. officials told Reuters that Gilman was being flown home on a State Department aircraft and would be met in Washington by special envoy Steve Witkoff, who was involved in efforts to secure his release.
From there, Gilman is expected to continue to a rehabilitation facility in San Antonio, Texas.
American organizations involved in efforts to free him warned last week that his condition had sharply worsened following alleged abuse in prison.
They said Gilman had entered a near-catatonic state and was barely responding to external stimuli.
One U.S. official told Reuters, however, that he had spoken with Gilman since his release and that he was now walking and talking.
“Considering the circumstances, he appears to be doing well,” the official said.
Reuters reported that four doctors were aboard the flight to the United States monitoring his condition.
Gilman’s mother, Nina, was also on the plane and had been reunited with her son.
The release came amid growing concern over Gilman’s health.
Until recently, he had been held in a prison in Voronezh, about 547 kilometers south of Moscow. Reports said that in late June he was transferred from the prison hospital to the psychiatric ward of a civilian hospital after entering a near-catatonic state diagnosed as dissociative stupor.
The condition can involve a profound reduction, or even complete disappearance, of voluntary movement and normal responses to outside stimuli.
Eric Lebson, a senior official with Global Reach, which represents Gilman’s family, said last Thursday that Gilman could no longer eat on his own and was being fed through a tube.
“We are very concerned that we could see another case like Otto Warmbier,” Lebson said.
Warmbier was an American student imprisoned in North Korea after being accused of trying to steal a propaganda poster. He was returned to the United States in June 2017 in a coma after 17 months in detention and died later that month from severe brain damage without regaining consciousness.
A person familiar with the case told Reuters that Secretary of State Marco Rubio raised Gilman’s case with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov during a meeting in Manila on July 23.
The source did not know how Lavrov responded.
Gilman’s sister, Lexi Hudson, who warned last week that her brother could die if he was not released soon, thanked Trump on Tuesday.
“I am so incredibly grateful to President Trump for saving my brother’s life,” she said.
“There is no other reason Robert is alive today except that President Trump heard about the case and took action.”
Gilman served in the U.S. Marine Corps from August 2019 to August 2020.
He was arrested in Voronezh in January 2022 while traveling by train. Russian authorities said he kicked a police officer while drunk.
His family has given a different account, saying that after being taken to a police station, Gilman vomited and accidentally kicked an officer during the incident.
The officer was not injured and did not ask to press charges, according to the family, but Gilman was prosecuted and sentenced to four and a half years in prison. His sentence was later reduced on appeal to three and a half years.
U.S. lawmakers argued that although five years is the maximum sentence in Russia for such an offense, Russian citizens convicted in similar cases typically receive a fine, suspended sentence or, in more serious cases, up to a year in prison.
Gilman’s prison term was later repeatedly extended.
In October 2024, he was convicted of assaulting a prison staff member and a government investigator and received a total sentence of seven years and one month.
He admitted to the charges but said he had resorted to violence after a staff member caused him pain in his genitals and after an investigator insulted his father, Vladimir Gilman, who had emigrated from Russia to Massachusetts.
In April 2025, another year was added to his term, bringing the sentence to eight years and one month.
According to Russian state media reports, Gilman was convicted in December 2025 of further assaults on prison staff, raising the total sentence to 10 years.
Organizations supporting the family have not necessarily denied that some of the incidents took place, but they argue that they resulted from severe and prolonged abuse.
They say Gilman was held in harsh conditions, tortured and forced to take mind-altering substances, with his health deteriorating until he was transferred to the civilian hospital.
His relatives have previously expressed suspicion that the alleged abuse was intended to provoke him into violent reactions, allowing authorities to keep extending his sentence and potentially turn him into leverage for a future prisoner exchange.

Trump also hurled another tirade against people of Somali descent, of which there are upwards of 260,000 across the US. He called them “not smart”, and said they have “no aptitude” and “nothing going” for them to “tell us how to run our country”.
Edward Ahmed Mitchell, the national deputy director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), a Muslim civil rights and advocacy organisation in the US, said that Trump’s hateful anti-Muslim rhetoric “is putting a target on the back of Muslim elected officials across our nation” and that “this type of dangerous rhetoric is fueling the surge in complaints of anti-Muslim bigotry that our civil rights organization has documented over the past three years”.
Although the president refrained from explicitly naming any individual candidate, hours later, he focused his attention on El-Sayed, who is a son of Egyptian immigrants. The president shared a photo on Truth Social showing the Democratic contender positioned before a gathering that featured two women in headscarves, accompanied by the caption: “They are coming for your home and your belongings.”
Trump also targeted El-Sayed’s victory directly last week, calling him a “hater of Jews” and “hater of Israel” who will bring “filth, crime, death, destruction, embarrassment”.
Several other Republicans also beefed up their anti-Muslim rhetoric, following El-Sayed’s win, parroting remarks that Muslims do not belong in American society. This outburst occurred just two days after Trump shared a social media post comparing a photo of himself and First Lady Melania Trump with one of El-Sayed and his wife Dr Sarah Jukaku, who is a psychiatrist. The image was captioned: “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s.”
Speaking on CNN’s State of the Union with host Jake Tapper on Sunday night, the Democratic Senate candidate hit back, saying, “Sarah and I actually like each other”, adding “I don’t know about the first lady and the president, but from what I’ve heard, it’s a bit of a rocky road”.
With less than 90 days to go until the highly anticipated midterm elections come to a head, and with all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 34 Senate seats up for grabs, Democrats are confronting an ideological schism between moderate leaders and triumphing democratic progressives, some of whom are increasingly being characterised as an endangerment to Washington’s national security establishment altogether.
“People don’t want to have radical lunatics involved in running our country,” said Trump on Monday, “and that’s what we have.”

DARPA Looks to Develop Next-Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:11:04 UTC
05:11:04 KST

The Pentagon’s top research lab is interested in developing a hypersonic cruise missile prototype that provides “a revolutionary leap in operational performance,” as the first wave of U.S. hypersonic weapons enters production and service.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency released a notice Aug. 7, informing industry of a potential new program called the Next-Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile and seeking information and ideas on the topic.
“The goal is to design, build, and flight-test a fully integrated hypersonic cruise missile system demonstrator,” the notice states. “This demonstrator must establish the foundation for a next-generation capability that delivers a revolutionary leap in operational performance—specifically in range, cruise speed, and/or altitude. This capability must maintain technological superiority, enabling the U.S. to promptly strike advanced threats in highly contested environments.”
The notice also states that previous demonstrator programs have proven the technology behind air-breathing hypersonic weapons. But these concepts have provided only “predictable, incremental gains in isolated performance metrics” and are often expensive and complex, making them hard to transition to mass production.
Now, DARPA is hoping for a “quantum leap in overall system performance,” fueled by “high-risk, high-reward technologies,” though the notice doesn’t say what those technologies might be.
In addition to range and speed, the agency is interested in improved performance in areas like midcourse maneuverability and overall signature so that the new hypersonic missile can better evade adversaries’ integrated air and missile defenses.
DARPA previously explored hypersonic cruise missiles through its Hypersonic Air-breathing Weapon Concept in the early 2020s, developed with the Air Force and Lockheed Martin and resulting in several successful flight tests. Then the Air Force started developing the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile with Raytheon—the service is planning to start production on the HACM in 2027, according to budget documents.
These weapons use a “scramjet” air-breathing engine to reach hypersonic speeds, defined as above Mach 5. They’re different from other “boost-glide” weapons that use solid rocket boosters to power the vehicle to hypersonic speeds and then have the vehicle coast or “glide” to its target while being able to maneuver along the way. Air-breathing weapons are considered more efficient and can be smaller, allowing them to be carried on a greater variety of platforms.
Indeed, DARPA’s latest notice states that the agency is interested in different “classes” of next-gen hypersonic missiles, ranging all the way from weapons that can be carried internally and externally on fighters to ones that can be launched from pallets to ones that can only be launched from bombers or on the ground.
In addition to developing a new generation of weapons, DARPA wants to develop new test and evaluation technologies for hypersonic weapons—testing has been a persistent chokepoint in hypersonics development.
Current Hypersonic Weapons
The Air Force is pouring most of is resources for hypersonics into the HACM program; the service’s 2027 budget request includes around $1.01 billion for HACM, split $404 million for production and $806 million for research, development, test, and evaluation. Exactly how expensive each of these missile are—and thus how many the Air Force is buying—remains secret.
The first aircraft HACM will be fielded on is the F-15E Strike Eagle, according to budget documents, and it could be carried by fighters and bombers alike.
But the service is also still pursuing the Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon. ARRW is a boost-glide weapon that can only be carried by bombers. Despite a series of test failures several years ago, the Air Force recently revived the program and is requesting $797 million for it in 2027: $452 million in procurement, $345 million in R&D mostly for a second “increment” of the weapon.
The Army and Navy, meanwhile, are working to field variants of the same boost-glide system called the Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon or Dark Eagle.

Air Force Wants a Drone Factory in a Box for Rapid, Remote Deployments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:10:25 UTC
05:10:25 KST

The Air Force wants to step up its ability to field unmanned systems with deployable manufacturing equipment for turning out small drones in austere terrain.
The service’s Rapid Sustainment Office, or RSO, is asking industry to submit ideas for creating expeditionary manufacturing equipment for producing and maintaining Group 1 and 2 drones—quadcopter-sized systems weighing up to 55 pounds—for reconnaissance, attack, and counter-drone missions.
The RSO, which is part of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center, is searching for “existing solutions for an on-demand manufacturing capability for ready-to-fly Unmanned Aerial Systems, purpose-built attritable systems, first-person-view drone build kits, counter UAS systems—such as interceptors—accessories, spare parts and supplies that can be operated in remote and austere environments,” according to an Aug. 7 request for information.
“This will allow for the rapid, persistent, and distributed production of unmanned air systems near the point of need reducing reliance on traditional supply chains and enabling forces to quickly replenish critical assets in contested areas.”
The RFI, which requires interested firms to submit a response by Aug. 28, is another step in the Air Force’s march to become more self-sufficient at defending its air bases from drones and other aerial threats. Currently, the service relies primarily on the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems. SUADS is designed to identify, track, and down drones and is available in two variants, one for fixed air bases and one that can be rapidly deployed on an aircraft pallet for rapid-deployment missions to austere areas of the battlefield.
SUADS is also designed to accept add-on counter-drone technologies, ranging from kinetic effectors to high-power microwave systems. The service is acquiring and fielding different types of counter-drone effectors as well as command and control systems through the Joint Interagency Task Force 401, Michael Sheehy, director of future operations under the Air Force deputy chief of staff for operations, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July.
But beyond SUADS, the Air Force is eyeing more small expendable drone systems faster that can be quickly replaced on remote battlefields.
Currently, the Air Force “does not have a preferred production capacity” but instead is interested in “scalable” expeditionary manufacturing equipment that can be loaded into a shipping container and transported by “C-130, cargo ship, and helicopter sling-load,” according to the RFI.
Interested defense firms should provide detailed descriptions of their expeditionary manufacturing capabilities such as “additive manufacturing/3D printing” and rapid assembly as well as “concepts for effective assembly solutions to include but not limited to soldering, battery wiring, and motor assembly,” the RFI states.
The Rapid Sustainment Office wants to hear from companies that can adapt to multiple “vendor agnostic compatible materials” and components with minimal reconfiguration, the solicitation states.
“This capability is aimed at being as agile as possible or to be drone agnostic but compatible with highly desirable materials commonly used in additive manufacturing,” the RFI states.
Each vendor’s manufacturing equipment and the components for assembling small drones should be compatible with standard military generators or tactical microgrids and must be able operate despite extreme environmental factors such as dust, humidity, temperatures ranging from minus 40 degrees to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, the solicitation states.
The office also wants to vendors to detail their “supply chain and logistics capabilities to maintain a continual UAS manufacturing stream that is free of components or software from China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, or any country that is a state sponsor of terrorism,” the RFI states.
The Air Force began focusing on creating a point defense strategy to deal with drone threats in late 2023 when unidentified drones flew unchecked for days over Langley Air Force Base, Va. More drone incursions followed at bases in Ohio, Utah, and the United Kingdom.
Since then, the service has launched initiatives such as publishing a new doctrine on the “Point Defense of Air Bases,” to ensure the service plays a more active role in air defense, a mission that has traditionally been an Army responsibility. The Air Force also stood up the Point Defense Task Force and Point Defense Battle Lab to develop to identify new training, equipment and tactics needed for the new mission.
The service has also created its first point defense flights, specialized units of Airmen trained to rapidly deploy to the Pacific and other hotspots and defend future remote air bases from drone attack. In the long-term, the service is developing a new job specialty code for base defense as the first step in developing this new career field.

The Iraqi government seeks to restrict weapons exclusively to the state and strengthen the authority of security institutions as part of its efforts to consolidate internal stability and avoid the repercussions of regional tensions.

On Monday, government spokesman Haider al-Aboudi said discussions are ongoing to overcome obstacles related to placing weapons under state control.

Qatar welcomes new Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani defense pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:06:50 UTC
05:06:50 KST

Hussien Elkabany and Mohammad Sio
11 August 2026•Update: 11 August 2026
Qatar on Tuesday welcomed the Mecca Mutual Defense Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan, saying it views positively any defense framework based on cooperation and good neighbor relations.
“We welcome any regional cooperation that strengthens security, stability and defense among the countries of the region,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al-Ansari told a weekly news conference in Doha.
“Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye are countries with which we have strategic relations and fraternal ties based on a shared destiny and common concerns,” he added.
“For the security of our region and the security of the world, we fully positively view any defense framework based on cooperation and good-neighborly relations,” Al-Ansari said.
He stressed that “regional security is a collective responsibility that requires regional coordination and cooperation.”
Last Friday, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the pact in the holy city of Mecca.
The agreement is part of defense cooperation that does not target any country but seeks to strengthen commitments to preserving peace, stability, and prosperity at the regional and global levels, based on burden-sharing and a common understanding of security.
It aims to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack on any of the three countries would be considered an attack pm all three.
The agreement also includes defense arrangements under which the three countries will support one another's security, develop cooperation in the defense industry, and enhance military interoperability.

‘Only God can save this country’: HC bins plea of J&amp;K cop sacked for skipping duty over terror threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:05:58 UTC
05:05:58 KST

"Engagement of SPOs is not of a permanent nature but only to take care of a particular contingency,” the HC noted.
Srinagar: Only God can save this country if a police officer, of whatever rank, gets frightened by terrorists’ threats and refuses duties, J&K high court has said while dismissing a cop’s petition for reinstatement.“The justification provided by the petitioner for not attending his duties is unacceptable, to say the least,” a single bench of Justice Sanjay Dhar said in its Monday order. The judge rejected special police officer (SPO) Hemo Hamid Wani’s argument that he was entitled to the “same powers, privileges and protections available to ordinary officers of police under Police Act”. The HC pointed out that “SPOs do not hold any civil posts regulated by statutory rules”.Residents of a neighbourhood are appointed SPOs “for specific purposes when the force ordinarily employed for preserving peace is not sufficient”. “Thus, engagement of SPOs is not of a permanent nature but only to take care of a particular contingency,” the HC noted.Wani was engaged as an SPO in 2012. In 2015, he was posted at Reshipora in south Kashmir’s Shopian. While at home on medical leave at one point then, he received life threats from terrorists and failed to report back to duties.
When he returned after some time to his posting, he was not allowed to join duty, forcing him to take the matter to senior officers.When no action was taken, Wani moved the HC. In Aug last year, the court directed the J&K police DGP to take a decision on Wani’s plea. The DGP turned it down, forcing Wani to move the HC again.In his HC petition, Wani argued that J&K Police had disengaged him without inquiry, formal charges or hearing. The action, he said, violated the Constitution’s Articles 16 (equality of opportunity in public employment), 21 (right to life and livelihood) and 311 (protection against arbitrary dismissal), besides provisions of J&K Police Rules.
The HC rejected the contentions, saying Wani, as an SPO, was not entitled to any hearing or inquiry in view of the temporary nature of his engagement. Even if it is assumed that Wani had the right to such a hearing, his failure to perform duties in the face of terror threats is enough reason to remove him, the HC held.“Granting an opportunity to the petitioner to present his case prior to disengagement would have been an empty formality. The DGP has rightly rejected the petitioner’s representation. The order does not call for any interference,” Justice Dhar observed.

Bolsonaro campaign drafts debt-linked fiscal rule to replace Brazil framework, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
20:04:37 UTC
05:04:37 KST

Bolsonaro campaign drafts debt-linked fiscal rule to replace Brazil framework, sources say
BRASILIA, Aug 11 - Senator Flavio Bolsonaro's presidential campaign is preparing a new fiscal framework to replace Brazil's current budget rules, imposing tighter spending caps as debt rises that could reduce real spending growth to zero, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The senator, who is the eldest son of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro, is the leading right-wing challenger to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the October election.
Brazil's gross public debt climbed to 81.9% of gross domestic product in June, compared to 71.4% when Lula took office in January 2023, leading many economists to flag the need for a painful fiscal adjustment by the next government.
Under Bolsonaro's draft proposal, spending growth would remain below revenue growth, while varying according to public debt levels. The higher the debt burden, the tighter the cap on spending growth, said the sources on condition of anonymity.
Depending on the final design, the rule could effectively freeze federal spending in real terms in the next administration. The exact parameters of the proposal are still being drafted, the sources said.
The proposal, floated by Bolsonaro advisers in private meetings with investors, could be sent to Congress as a constitutional amendment during a potential government transition later this year, sources said.
The framework would replace Lula's fiscal rules, which currently cap real spending growth at between 0.6% and 2.5% annually and limit it to no more than 70% of revenue growth.
In response to a Reuters request for comment, the Bolsonaro campaign said its government platform would be released by August 15, the deadline set by electoral law, and would detail its economic proposals.
His proposals will aim to strengthen fiscal discipline, improve public-sector efficiency and create conditions for stronger economic growth, the campaign added.
One source said the proposal, still under discussion, could freeze federal spending in real terms whenever gross government debt exceeds 80% of GDP, a threshold that has already been breached. Spending growth would be limited to 50% of revenue growth when debt stands between 75% and 80% of GDP, rising to 70% of revenue growth when debt falls below 75% of GDP, the source added.
The framework would also include a primary balance target and a spending cap, a mechanism already present under Lula's current rules, although the precise levels have yet to be determined.
Alongside the overhaul, Bolsonaro's team is preparing spending cuts and a review of tax breaks aimed at delivering a fiscal adjustment equivalent to 1.5% of GDP, said the two sources. The goal is to boost investor confidence, lower long-term interest rates and generate additional fiscal gains, one of them added. REUTERS
