Federal report says firefighting tactics at Maine lumber mill explosion aided the blast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:23:01 UTC
04:23:01 KST

Federal report says firefighting tactics at Maine lumber mill explosion aided the blast
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — Firefighters who responded to a deadly fire at a Maine lumber mill used tactics that inadvertently helped cause an explosion, according to a report from federal investigators.
The May 15 fire and explosion killed three people, including two firefighters, and originated at the base of a silo, Maine authorities have said. The blast at Robbins Lumber in rural Searsmont also injured at least 13 people and the toppling of the silo engulfed the surrounding area in fire, they have said.
The silo was an oxygen-limiting structure, according to a report released by National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health this month. At the scene, firefighters flowed water into the silo, though the manufacturer’s emergency procedures warn against that, the report said.
“The document warns against spraying water or foam into the oxygen-limiting silo as it will force air in and may create a potentially explosive mixture,” the report states. “The application of water into the silo in this incident likely entrained oxygen into the silo headspace, stirred up dust within the contents, and caused it to become suspended in an explosive concentration.”
The report states in its recommendations that fire departments should make sure firefighters choose appropriate tactics for silo fires and never direct water or foam into oxygen-limiting silos. It also states that more training is needed for fire departments about the hazards associated with different types of silos.
The explosion took place in the small town about 95 miles (150 kilometers) northeast of Portland and triggered a response of 299 firefighters from 46 departments across a four-county area. It took them hours to contain the fire.
Representatives for Searsmont Fire & Rescue did not return phone calls seeking comment Tuesday. The department’s assistant fire chief, Wayne Woodbury, 76, died from injuries suffered in the explosion. Andrew Cross, 27, of the Morrill Volunteer Fire Department, also died. Alden Robbins, the co-owner of the mill, died from injuries weeks later.
Robbins Lumber representatives said on the company’s website that “no report can fully capture the heartbreak experienced by our community, nor can it lessen the tremendous loss suffered by so many.” The company is working with industry experts to rebuild its facilities, the statement said.
“Our objective is not simply to meet current industry standards, but to exceed them. We are committed to learning from this event and to doing everything we can to help prevent anything like this from happening again,” the statement said.
The National Fire Protection Association declined to comment on the report beyond saying it encourages firefighters to participate in National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health’s work to improve safety investigations. The Maine Department of Public Safety also declined to comment.
The Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office said in late May that rapid ignition of particulate material resulted in the silo explosion, which caused it to lift from its concrete base and release large amounts of sawdust and other materials. It said the fire and explosion were accidental.
The mill is a part of the historic lumber and wood products industry in Maine. The company has said it is a high tech lumber manufacturer that has been in existence since the 19th century.

Syrian officials hail death sentences against Assad regime figures as victory for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:21:52 UTC
04:21:52 KST

- Officials say verdicts mark  step toward accountability and transitional justice
Syrian officials on Tuesday welcomed death sentences handed down against several senior figures of the ousted Bashar al-Assad regime, describing the verdicts as reflecting the will of the Syrian people, a victory for justice and a rejection of impunity.
Earlier Tuesday, the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus sentenced Brig. Gen. Atef Najib, the former head of the Political Security branch in the southern province of Daraa, to death.
It also handed down death sentences in absentia to Bashar al-Assad, the deposed regime leader and Najib’s cousin; Maher al-Assad, his brother and former commander of the Fourth Division; and six other former security and military officials who remain at large.
The court found them guilty of “crimes against humanity,” intentional killing, torture and arbitrary detention.
‘Just punishment’
Commenting on the verdicts, Interior Minister Anas Khattab said: “Today, justice has prevailed for the victims of crimes and violations committed against Syrians,” according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
“Congratulations to the Syrian people on the issuance of the first death sentences against the perpetrators of these crimes, in a historic step toward redressing victims and holding those responsible accountable,” Khattab said.
“We will continue pursuing everyone involved in these crimes until they receive their just punishment,” he added.
Information Minister Khaled Zaarour said the death sentences against the “leaders of the former regime” represent “another victory for Syrians and a definitive confirmation that there will be no impunity,” according to SANA.
He said transitional justice and national efforts are “the real guarantee of the rights of the victims of the Syrian revolution and the cornerstone for closing the era of authoritarianism and building a new Syria.”
Awqaf Minister Mohammad Abu al-Khair Shukri said the verdicts represent “a new step toward consolidating the rule of law and justice, providing redress to victims and restoring rights to their owners,” according to SANA.
‘Independent judiciary’
Justice Minister Mazhar al-Wais said the verdicts against “criminals of the former regime” followed a series of judicial proceedings and were issued “in the name of the Syrian people,” Syrian Alikhbariah TV reported.
Al-Wais said Syrians had decided to build their new state on “justice, citizenship and the rule of law.” He called on citizens to trust state institutions and the national process launched after the fall of the former regime and seek their rights through the relevant institutions.
He said the verdicts were issued in accordance with Syrian penal law and international humanitarian law as part of efforts to provide redress to victims and prevent impunity.
He also stressed that “the Syrian judiciary is independent,” adding that the Justice Ministry and the Supreme Judicial Council were responsible for removing obstacles and ensuring the judiciary had the resources it needed.
Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said the death sentence represents “an important milestone on the path to justice and accountability for those responsible for crimes and violations against the Syrian people.”
He said transitional justice would continue to hold accountable anyone whose hands were “stained with the blood of Syrians,” regardless of position or rank, to establish a state based on law and justice.
SANA also quoted Syrian Bar Association head Mohammad Ali al-Tawil as saying the ruling was “a historic landmark” in the country’s judicial history and a legal culmination of the patience of mothers of those killed and wounded, as well as a tribute to victims of years of oppression and suffering affecting millions of Syrians.
“There will be no position or authority in the new Syria above the voice of law and justice,” al-Tawil said, adding that the judiciary is moving toward a more sustainable process of healing the country’s wounds.
‘Deterrent punishment’
Hama Governor Abdul Rahman al-Suhyan said: “Today, justice has spoken,” adding that Hama, “the province that knew the meaning of injustice and deprivation,” affirmed that justice is the foundation for building a new Syria, according to SANA.
Tartous Governor Ahmad al-Shami described the death sentence against “war criminals” as “a deterrent punishment for what they committed against humanity, restoring dignity to every victim and providing solace to the mothers of the missing,” according to SANA.
The ruling demonstrated that “justice, however long it takes, will come, and that the truth does not die no matter how much falsehood conspires against it,” he added.
Celebrations in Daraa
Later, SANA reported that residents of Daraa gathered in the courtyard of the Omari Mosque in the Daraa al-Balad neighborhood to celebrate the death sentence against Najib and other former regime figures.
Participants held signs reading, among other slogans: “Truth has prevailed and falsehood has perished,” “Daraa, birthplace of the revolution, has prevailed again,” and “The blood of the martyrs will not be lost.”
The Omari Mosque was the site of a deadly crackdown by former regime forces during the early days of the Syrian revolution, when troops stormed the mosque and killed and wounded dozens of worshippers.
The public prosecution and the prosecution authority had called for the maximum punishment, death, against Najib and the other defendants who remain at large, including Bashar and Maher al-Assad.
The case centers on Najib’s role in suppressing protests in Daraa, where the Syrian uprising began on March 18, 2011, after several children were arrested and tortured for writing anti-regime slogans on walls.
Najib was also linked to the storming of the Omari Mosque and the humiliation of local residents. The US and EU placed him on their sanctions lists in April and May 2011, respectively.
The trial, whose first hearings began on April 26, represents a major step in Syria’s transitional justice process following the capture of Damascus by Syrian opposition factions on Dec. 8, 2024, ending 61 years of Baath Party rule, including 53 years under the Assad family.

Putin Demands Private Business Fund Russian Science as War Drains Federal Budget
Russian leader Vladimir Putin is urging private domestic companies to finance scientific development as state funding declines amid heavy defense spending.
One out of every three federal rubles is currently directed toward Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as reported by The Moscow Times on August 11.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to data from the Institute for Statistical Studies and Economics of Knowledge at the Higher School of Economics (ISSEK HSE), the federal budget allocated 792.1 billion rubles ($8.7 billion) to civilian science last year.
This accounted for only 2.5% of total government expenditure, making it 22 times smaller than the 17.8 trillion rubles ($195.8 billion) spent combined on the military and security forces.
Speaking at a meeting of the Council for Science and Education in Novosibirsk, Putin stated that commercial enterprises must directly commission technological developments.
"We need to set up the work in such a way that domestic business and enterprises act as direct customers of breakthrough scientific solutions and technologies. Taking clear obligations to create successful, competitive products based on them," Putin said.
He added, "To achieve practical, truly breakthrough results, maximum concentration of efforts of all participants in Russia's scientific and technological development is needed."
Although nominal federal funding for research grew by 11% over the past year, real expenditure adjusted for inflation dropped 14% below pre-war levels. Compared to 2013, real scientific funding has fallen by 25%. Spending as a share of gross domestic product reached 15-year lows, dropping to 0.35% of GDP in 2024 and 0.37% in 2025.
Initiative programs for technological leadership announced by Putin were left without funding following a federal budget deficit that reached 5.6 trillion rubles ($61.6 billion) where the gap expanded.
The primary space exploration initiative received no funding despite an original allocation plan of 10 billion rubles ($110 million). Funding for the automated production and robotics program was reduced by 75%, while funding for chemical development, new materials, and transport mobility projects was cut by 40%.
During the first nine months of 2025, Russia spent $146.4 billion from its budget on military expenditures—four times more than in 2021—which accounted for 39% of total government spending.
Meanwhile, the federal budget deficit grew to $69.8 billion in 2025, prompting the Kremlin to cover its widening fiscal gap by requiring state-controlled banks to purchase $87 billion in federal loan bonds backed by Central Bank liquidity.

US company stokes Greenland tensions by unloading drilling gear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:11:01 UTC
04:11:01 KST

US company stokes Greenland tensions by unloading drilling gear
- A US energy company unloaded drilling equipment in Greenland without authorisation, causing tensions amid fears of US territorial ambitions.
- Greenland's government issued a strong warning, emphasising all future activities need prior approval and noting environmental and social concerns.
- Local residents protested the project, which faces delays due to missing impact studies and harsh Arctic conditions, despite potential large oil reserves.
AI generated
COPENHAGEN - A US energy exploration company has sparked an outcry by unloading drilling equipment without authorisation on the east coast of Greenland, the autonomous Danish territory coveted by US President Donald Trump.
Texas-based Greenland Energy - which insists it has no connection to the US president’s territorial ambitions - maintains that it was merely taking a preliminary step towards exploration activities when it unloaded the gear in July in Nunap Qeqqa, also known as Jameson Land.
Greenland Energy did not respond to an AFP request for comment, but it told Danish media in July that it believed that authorisation to unload and store its equipment, which was located in another part of Greenland, was only required within the oil exploration licence area.
“It was a mistake on our part, a mistake that will not be repeated,” its managing director, Roderick McIllree, told Danish public broadcaster DR in late July.
The equipment is currently stored in a hangar at Nerlerit Inaat Airport, near the village of Ittoqqortoormiit, the closest settlement to the licence area.
The company has received a “strong warning” from the Greenland government, which in a statement in July added “that all future logistical arrangements must be notified to and approved by the mineral resources authority before they are carried out”.
Greenland Energy’s chairman, Larry Swets, has been described as being close to Trump.
And at a time when the US president still wishes to control the vast Arctic island, the prospect of a US energy company potentially carrying out exploration activities is making people uneasy.
“There is this vague sense of a connection to Trump,” Ulrik Pram Gad, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, told AFP.
‘Anxiety’
“This creates anxiety and tensions, all the more so because with Trump you can expect anything,” he added.
“With this unauthorised unloading of equipment, the company has really not improved its chances with the Greenland authorities,” said Anne Merrild, a professor at Aalborg University and Arctic specialist.
In 2021, the Greenlandic government, which manages the island’s natural resources, declared a moratorium on the exploration and extraction of oil across the Arctic territory, which has been profoundly disrupted by climate change.
But the exploration licences under which Greenland Energy operates were issued earlier, in 2015 and 2018, and therefore remain valid.
“One of the conditions for keeping the licence is to actively explore the area,” Pram Gad pointed out, while noting that “the company is under pressure”, as it is not active currently.
Activities are subject to specific permits, and Greenland Energy still hopes to obtain full approval to begin drilling soon in order to determine the quality of potential deposits.
There is a need to double down on preparations and equipment on land that is inherently hostile due to the harsh Arctic conditions.
“We continue to be encouraged by the progress being made toward the remaining approvals required for drilling,” Greenland Energy said in a letter to shareholders.
Greenland’s government is less optimistic.
“Given the current situation, I do not consider it realistic that the company can drill in the autumn,” Greenland Foreign Minister Mute Egede, who is responsible for natural resources, told the territory’s broadcaster, KNR.
Global tensions
The environmental and social impact studies required to approve the project have not yet been submitted, the Greenland government has noted.
“The few inhabitants of the region depend on the surrounding nature: they are hunters, fishers,” Merrild explained.
“Drilling causes a lot of disturbance, and increased human activity would have an impact on wildlife.”
In Ittoqqortoormiit, more than a hundred people – out of the 325 inhabitants of the village – demonstrated in mid-July against the project, according to KNR.
The geological survey of Denmark and Greenland (GEUS) estimates that the region could contain the equivalent of 2.35 billion barrels of oil, a considerable volume for a single oil project, but limited when compared with reserves around the globe.
“In the company’s logic, given current geopolitical tensions, the project sends a signal; it’s a way of saying ‘we have access to resources elsewhere’,” Merrild stressed. AFP

New Security Operation “VILKATIS” Began in Latvia’s Eastern Border Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11

04:09:38 KST

Following the initiative of Prime Minister of Latvia Andris Kulbergs and an assessment of the situation by the defence and interior ministries, a decision has been made to launch Operation “VILKATIS” to ensure the security of Latvia’s eastern border. The operation is coordinated by the Crisis Management Centre of the State Chancellery, while its implementation primarily involves agencies under the Ministry of the Interior (the State Border Guard and the State Police) and the National Armed Forces.
The Ministry of Defence will ensure the continued involvement of the National Armed Forces in support of the State Border Guard by increasing personnel and material resources, including the use of new technologies such as unmanned aerial vehicles (drones), helicopters, and aircraft.
The State Border Guard, State Police, Military Intelligence and Security Service, State Security Service, and National Armed Forces will ensure the exchange of operational information regarding attempts at illegal border crossings and the persons involved, including possible involvement in organizing illegal migration.
As part of the operation, modern technologies will be used more intensively for the detection and detention of illegal migrants, as well as for the protection of Latvia’s entire eastern border. Unmanned aerial systems will be deployed more extensively in border areas to improve the early detection of illegal migrants and facilitate their detention if the border has been crossed unlawfully.
To address more effectively hybrid threats against Latvia and strengthen border-control capabilities, on 11 August 2026 the Cabinet of Ministers will decide on the establishment of a special working group with specific tasks. This will enhance the effectiveness of measures to prevent border violations and ensure coordinated and harmonized action with Lithuania, Estonia, Poland, and other countries in the region.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs will ensure cooperation and coordination with Lithuania, Estonia, and Poland regarding the prevention of illegal border crossings and secondary migration flows at the diplomatic level.
The Ministry of Justice will assess whether the sanctions provided for in the Criminal Law for organizing illegal border crossings, facilitating unlawful residence in Latvia, and fraudulently facilitating the acquisition of legal residence rights are sufficient.
Illegal migration is an instrument of hybrid warfare and a deliberate provocation against Latvia as one of the states forming the external border of the European Union and NATO. The instrumentalization of migration by Russia and Belarus as a form of hybrid threat has led to a disproportionately high and growing number of illegal border-crossing incidents. Limiting illegal migration is a shared responsibility of all relevant institutions.
A special border-security regime has been declared until 31 December 2026 in Ludza Municipality, Krāslava Municipality, Augšdaugava Municipality, the state city of Daugavpils, and Kaunata Parish in Rēzekne Municipality.

Coalition pushes VIP gambling crackdown in talks with Labor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:00:53 UTC
04:00:53 KST

Limited gambling changes on the table in Coalition, Labor talks
In short:
Labor and the Coalition have held a second round of "constructive" talks on the federal government's proposal to restrict gambling advertising, making a major party deal likely.
Negotiations have focused on VIP inducements, protections for self-excluded gamblers and online advertising rules, while there are also calls for an independent review.
What's next?
The federal government is hoping to get its gambling legislation through the Senate in the next fortnight, meaning the Coalition party room would have to sign off on a final deal within days.
The Coalition is seeking a targeted crackdown on VIP gambling inducements offered to high rollers and a simplified option to curb ads on streaming services amid ongoing "constructive" gambling bill talks with the federal government.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met early Tuesday evening for a second time in as many days to hash out details of an expected agreement to amend Labor’s proposed gambling ad restrictions.
Major changes such as an "opt-in" system for online advertising or a total ban on so-called gambling inducements are not on the table from either side, with Mr Albanese having previously indicated he would not entertain a wholesale rewrite of the draft legislation.
Instead, the asks put forward by Mr Taylor and Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson have focused on stronger protections for children and vulnerable people from exposure to advertising or predatory industry tactics.
With a modest deal seeming increasingly likely, gambling harm reduction advocates within the Coalition are calling for the bill to include an automatic independent review of the measures in the future.
It is hoped this would eventually expose what they believe are flaws in the legislation and create the case for further changes in the next term of government.
Labor is seeking to pass the legislation through the Senate by the end of the fortnight, which Mr Taylor is understood to be open to though is not in a rush this week as he has committed to take a final proposal back to the full Coalition party room for sign off.
Coalition asks for focus on high-end inducements
Rather than a broader crackdown on so-called gambling inducements, such as bonus bet offers, the Coalition has instead asked Labor for amendments focused on vulnerable and high-spending gamblers.
This included creating some type of cooling period preventing gambling companies from sending any inducements to Australians immediately after they remove themselves from the government’s self-exclusion register Betstop.
Loading...
The Opposition has also suggested targeting VIP offers extended to high rollers, such as access to exclusive events, game day tickets or large bonus-bet offers.
More common inducements pushed out to the average customer, such as deposit or bonus bet deals in the $25 range, are not the focus of the Coalition’s negotiations with Labor.
This is in part due to a view that the Liberals and Nationals must remain the parties of "personal responsibility" where individuals are expected to make their own decisions.
Coalition wants to give streamers option to comply with TV ad laws
The Coalition has also proposed a workaround for concerns among what has been dubbed a "triple lock" requiring all online platforms to restrict gambling ads to logged-in users who are aged over 18, while also giving every adult user a simple way to "opt out".
Harm advocates are unhappy with this proposal, because if a streaming service, social media or other online platform has a triple lock in place, they can show as many gambling ads as they want to over-aged, logged in viewers who have not opted out.
Streamers have also expressed concerns about the complexity of the proposed system.
The Coalition has therefore suggested streamers be given the option of either enforcing a triple lock or adopting the far more restrictive advertising rules for TV.
Under the bill, gambling ads are limited to three per hour between 6am and 8:30pm and banned during live sport broadcasts within those hours.
Liberal MP Simon Kennedy used a speech in parliament on Tuesday to attack the "two glaring problems" with Labor’s bill, which he said "did nothing" on inducements and allowed “unlimited advertising online” for adults who had not opted out.
"There should be an independent review of wherever we land after the next election, so we can do more," he said.
Inducements up for negotiation in ‘unusual’ leader talks
Coalition sources acknowledged it was "unusual" for Mr Taylor and Mr Albanese to meet twice to discuss legislative issues, attributing it to the prime minister's interest in being involved in negotiations.
Both leaders were on annual leave last week when a two-day Senate inquiry heard shocking evidence about the efforts VIP account managers at gambling companies went to strengthen relationships with high-rolling clients.
Allegations of offers to provide access to illicit drugs dominated media coverage of the hearings, but advocates also warned of harmful legal examples of so-called gambling inducements.
This included things like big spending gamblers being offered travel, accommodation and access to exclusive events linked to race days or football games.
Advocates also warned about the targeting of gamblers with inducements such as bonus bets, which the wagering sector described as “promotions”.
Last month Labor members unanimously voted to adopt a pledge to tackle these inducements into the party's 2026 national policy platform.
More than three years ago the You Win Some, You Lose More report into online wagering harms, which was authored by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy, recommended a total ban on all inducements.
Multiple Labor backbench MPs have gone public with their push for the party to address inducements since the government’s draft bill did not deal with the issue.
Industry expects 'unscrupulous' VIP account manager crackdown
Sources in the wagering industry said one of the issues discussed between the Coalition and Labor was a crackdown on the "payment" of VIP account managers offering gambling promotions.
At the Senate hearing last week, ACT independent Senator David Pocock was visibly shocked by evidence account managers at some wagering companies were paid on commission based on customers’ losses.
A wagering source said they believed Labor's bill could be amended to stop "unscrupulous" account managers being paid in this way.
This would not impact every company however, as the ABC reported last year that Sportsbet and Tabcorp no longer pay commissions to VIP account managers.
Any deal between Mr Taylor and Mr Albanese would still have to be signed off by the Coalition party room, which meets weekly when parliament is sitting.
Five backbenchers using the regular meeting on Tuesday to push for tougher reforms, while four cautioned against over-regulation.
Greens communications spokeswoman Senator Sarah Hanson-Young said Labor always intended to make a deal with the Coalition on the gambling reforms, to get away with doing the "bare minimum" on the issue.
Loading
Senator Hanson-Young said she met yesterday with Communications Minister Anika Wells, who indicated the government was willing to amend the bill to limit inducements.
"Last week, we were told the government wouldn't move at all and now they're saying they're prepared to move. The question is how far?" she said.
"The government has always intended to put this piece of legislation through with the opposition because they want to do the bare minimum.
"I have no faith that Angus Taylor is up to the job of negotiating the best outcome for people here."

The development comes as neighbouring Colombia has recognised Israel’s claim of sovereignty over the occupied Syrian Golan Heights, joining the US as the only other country to recognise Israel’s illegal annexation of the Syrian territory in 1981.
The UN recognises the region as a part of Syria, and UN chief Antonio Guterres has reiterated that stance, describing illegal Israeli occupation as "totally unacceptable".
Colombia’s government under then-President Gustavo Petro had severed diplomatic relations with Israel in May 2024 after months of tensions, with Petro saying he could not maintain ties with a genocidal government.
Bogota had also intervened in the genocide case against Israel, brought by South Africa before the International Court of Justice and supported by several other countries.

Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community feels misunderstood. Here’s why - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Over the last few years, the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) community has become the subject of every front page, television debate, and political confrontation in Israel.
Questions about Torah study, military service, education, employment, and the relationship between haredim and the state moved from the margins of public debate to the center of a national storm.
Much of that debate has presented Israelis with a false choice. Either the haredi community must be forced to change from the outside, or nothing can change at all. Either Israel protects the world of Torah, or it demands greater participation in the responsibilities of national life.
After spending a year listening to haredim across Israel, I am convinced that this choice is not only false but also dangerous. Change is possible. It is already desired by many within the haredi community.
Nonetheless, it will succeed only if it grows from within, with the support and partnership of the wider Israeli public.
I traveled across the country and met haredim from different communities, backgrounds, and stages of life. I spoke with those dedicated to full-time Torah study, working fathers, mothers struggling to support large families, educators, business owners, and young people trying to find their place.
I listened to people from hassidic, Lithuanian, and Sephardi communities, including those deeply connected to existing institutions and those who increasingly feel pushed to the margins.
The details differed, but the message was remarkably consistent: many haredim are deeply dissatisfied. They do not feel represented, and they do not believe their voices are being heard.
They feel trapped between two political camps, neither of which fully understands them. On one side are those who speak about the haredi community primarily as a demographic, economic, or security problem.
Their frustration is understandable, especially post-October 7, but solutions imposed without trust, cultural sensitivity, or an understanding of haredi life are unlikely to produce lasting change.
On the other side are the established haredi parties. For four decades, they have claimed a monopoly on haredi representation, but they have become more effective at preserving their own political power than confronting the mounting difficulties within haredi homes and communities.
The ultra-Orthodox are acutely aware of the dangers Israel faces
The people I met were not seeking to abandon Torah life. They wanted to protect it, but they also understood that refusing to confront reality is placing that future in danger.
They asked difficult and necessary questions.
How can a father support his family with dignity without feeling that earning a living will cost him his place in the community?
What future is being offered to a young man who is not suited to full-time Torah study? Why are educational and professional options so limited for those who need another path?
How can appropriate frameworks for military or national service be created for those who can serve without requiring them to sacrifice their religious identity?
How can genuine Torah scholars receive the respect and support they deserve while others receive the tools to build independent and productive lives?
These are not attacks on the world of Torah. Ignoring these questions is what threatens the world of Torah.
This year of listening led to the establishment of the Haredi Public Party. It is intended to provide a political home for haredim and others who believe that protecting Torah requires responsible leadership, honesty, and practical solutions.
We seek to strengthen genuine Torah study while expanding educational and professional opportunities. We want to enable dignified employment, develop appropriate frameworks for military or meaningful national service, address the needs of young people who do not fit the existing system, and help haredi families achieve greater economic independence.
Israelis outside the haredi community should care about this initiative because the future of the haredi community will have a great effect on the future of Israel.
The economic sustainability of the country, the strength of the IDF, the resilience of Israeli society, and our ability to remain one people all depend on finding workable answers to these questions.
Continued poverty, alienation, and political paralysis within a rapidly growing section of the population will not remain an internal haredi matter. Its consequences will affect every Israeli family.
Those who want greater haredi participation in employment, education, and national responsibility should therefore recognize an essential truth: the most sustainable transformation will come from haredim who possess the trust and cultural understanding to lead it.
Coercion may produce headlines, but it rarely produces lasting social change. At the same time, preserving the current political arrangement will only deepen the crisis.
If the established haredi parties were capable of providing meaningful answers to these challenges, they would have done so by now. Israel, therefore, needs a new approach: reform led from within the haredi community and supported through cooperation and coordination with the rest of Israeli society.
Secular Israelis, national-religious Israelis, or traditional Israelis do not have to agree with every aspect of haredi life, and legitimate questions about equality, military service, or public resources should not disappear. They all need meaningful and practical solutions.
Tolerance is key to sustaining healthy dynamic between religious and secular Jews
However, we must recognize that partnership is more likely to succeed than humiliation, and that responsible haredi leadership that can build bridges with other segments of Israeli society is in the national interest.
Even Israelis who would never vote for a haredi party should welcome the emergence of a haredi movement prepared to confront these issues honestly. They should want haredi representatives who speak of solutions rather than slogans, of responsibility rather than permanent victimhood, and of cooperation rather than endless confrontation.
A strong haredi community and a strong Israel are not competing goals. They depend upon one another. Israel needs a haredi community that is confident, economically secure, and able to contribute its values, energy, and talents to the country.
The haredi community needs an Israel that respects Torah, protects religious life, and treats haredim as partners rather than as a burden or an enemy.
We have spent too many years shouting past one another. The result has been greater poverty, deeper resentment, diminishing trust, and an increasingly dangerous struggle over Israel’s identity.
There is still a window in which to choose another path, but it will not remain open indefinitely.
The Haredi Public Party was created because the haredi public deserves more than excuses, and the State of Israel deserves more than permanent confrontation.
Those who care about Israel’s economic future, social cohesion, and national security should want this effort to succeed.
The solutions must emerge from within the haredi community, but they cannot succeed without the understanding and support of the wider Israeli public.
This affects far more than just the haredi community and is a necessity for the betterment of Israeli society as a whole.
The writer is the chairman of the Haredi Public Party, a new political home for haredim who believe that protecting the world of Torah requires responsible leadership and practical solutions to the challenges facing our community and all of Am Yisrael.

UNESCO says 2.4 million Afghan girls denied access to further education

UNESCO says 2.4 million Afghan girls denied access to further education
UNESCO says the figure could reach four million by 2030 unless Taliban reverses policy
About 2.4 million girls in Afghanistan are barred from secondary school, the United Nations cultural agency has said, renewing its call on the Taliban government to lift restrictions on female education.
UNESCO said on Tuesday that the number of girls deprived of secondary school in the country has grown by 200,000 since last year’s count, and could approach four million by 2030.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Taliban ban on girls’ education defies both worldly and religious logic
- list 2 of 3Is the Taliban-Russia MoU good for Afghanistan?
- list 3 of 3What Afghanistan’s rotten apples tell us about its non-profit sector
Afghanistan is the only country in the world to stop girls and women attending secondary schools and universities, among multiple restrictions on women that have led the UN to accuse the country of “gender apartheid”.
Girls were shut out of secondary schools in March 2022, while women were barred from universities in December that year, months after the Taliban returned to power as the US and allied troops ended their 20-year occupation of the country.
The Taliban administration also banned women from teaching boys, a measure which the UN says stripped qualified staff from the system and left boys with untrained male teachers. The agency projects a shortfall of more than 11,000 qualified female teachers by 2030.
The UN notes that the ban adds to a number of compounding issues weighing on Afghanistan’s education system and economy.
Many schools face overcrowding and are poorly equipped. Nearly half of schools lack water, sanitation or heating, and natural disasters have forced about a thousand schools to close in five years.
At the primary school level, more than two million children are out of class. Ninety percent of 10-year-olds cannot read a simple text, bringing national literacy down to 37 percent.
The Taliban government has rejected global calls, including from several Muslim-majority governments, to lift its ban on girls’ education, describing the policy as an internal matter.

Venezuela and Israel restore consular ties as relations warm
Despite cutting diplomatic ties with Israel in 2009, Caracas has shifted alignment in wake of Maduro abduction.

The announcement by both Israel and Venezuela on Tuesday comes as the interim President Delcy Rodriguez has pursued a major realignment since the United States military abduction of leader Nicolas Maduro in January.

That has included thawing ties with Israel, after Caracas severed ties 17 years ago in light of Israeli attacks on Gaza. Under Maduro, Venezuela had remained staunchly opposed to Israel, while aligning with regional foe Iran.

In a post on X, the Israeli government’s Spanish-language account said the change indicates “both governments recognise the importance of the bond between the State of Israel and the Jewish community residing in Venezuela, which constitutes an important historical bridge of friendship between the two countries”.

The approach represented a major pivot from his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro, who was among the region’s top critics of Israel.

====================================================================================================

Hundreds of teenagers waited hours outside Russia’s Supreme Court to witness the only antiwar party lose its place on the ballot. Then a police officer raised a megaphone to talk about draft offices.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:56:43 UTC
03:56:43 KST

Hundreds of teenagers waited hours outside Russia’s Supreme Court to witness the only antiwar party lose its place on the ballot. Then a police officer raised a megaphone to talk about draft offices.
All day on August 10, Russia’s Supreme Court heard a lawsuit seeking to revoke the Yabloko (“Apple”) party’s registration for the State Duma elections. Hundreds of people stood outside the courthouse on Povarskaya Street the entire time, supporters of the only antiwar party that could theoretically participate in the vote. Most were Muscovites under 30, many of them teenagers. For many of them, it was their first street protest; some were not even old enough to vote in September. They passed apples around, and in the evening they went home peacefully, though deflated by the court’s ruling. The independent journalists’ cooperative Bereg was there too. Meduza is translating Bereg’s report on what happened in central Moscow and what young Yabloko supporters had to say.
Hundreds of Russians turned out to support Yabloko at the courthouse. The audio version of Bereg’s dispatch from Moscow
Nikolai Rybakov, the chairman of Yabloko, arrived at Russia’s Supreme Court to a welcome better suited to a rock star: the crowd shouted and applauded, and people pressed in to shake his hand or at least to touch him.
The hearing was set to begin at 10 a.m. It ran all day, and it ended with the court barring Yabloko from the elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament. The suit was brought by the Rodina (“Motherland”) party, which listed a long roster of reasons Yabloko should be kept off the ballot. Four of them mattered most.
Rodina’s central complaint was that Yabloko had repeatedly violated copyright law in its campaign materials.
What exactly are Rodina's formal claims against Yabloko?
The problem, according to Rodina, lay mainly in Otkrovenny razgovor (“A Frank Conversation”), a series of interviews that the journalist Nikita Vasilenko conducts with Grigory Yavlinsky and that Yabloko publishes on its own website, among other places. In one of those videos, Rodina argued, the producers made unlawful use of:
- Images of Dmitry Medvedev and Victoria Bonya
- A shot from Sergei Bondarchuk’s film War and Peace
- A photograph of the aftermath of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima
- A line from the song “May There Always Be Sunshine,” used without the rights holder’s permission, and the phrase “anything, so long as there’s no war”
- Images from stock photo libraries
- Images generated by artificial intelligence
Rodina objected even to the party’s logo, which has barely changed since Yabloko was founded in 1993, saying it plagiarized “Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge,” the 1920 poster by the avant-garde artist El Lissitzky.
Rodina also argued that Yabloko should be barred from the race because too many people were campaigning for it online and because its campaign was allegedly financed from abroad. And it accused the party of extremism: Yabloko has spoken out against the persecution of LGBTQ+ people, and it has called for a ceasefire in the war in Ukraine — a demand Rodina treats as a call to violate Russia’s territorial integrity.
The courtroom seats 150, but half the seats sat empty: passes for spectators were issued too late. Hundreds turned out in front of the building anyway — at least 500, by Yabloko’s own count. Nearly all of them were under 30, and a good many were teenagers.
Those who couldn’t get into the courtroom watched the video feed on their phones. Some leaned back against the building’s facade; others sat on the curb or on the pavement. Several official cars and two prisoner transport vans were parked in the roadway, and patrols worked the sidewalks: ordinary police, OMON riot police, and Russian National Guard troops. The security officers didn’t cover their faces or tell anyone to disperse — they just talked quietly among themselves.
“Who’s on trial?” asked a boy of about 14, looking around curiously as he came up to a group of young people.
“The Yabloko party.”
“Ah, got it,” the teenager said, nodding. “Let’s see what happens!”
A young man ran up to the crowd with a sack of apples and handed them out to anyone who wanted one — including the teenager who had just joined the supporters.
Some had come prepared, in T-shirts and scarves with the party logo and accessories shaped like white doves and peace signs. Right by the courthouse doors stood a young woman in a straw hat with a blue ribbon, holding Viktor Vilisov‘s aptly titled book Nas vsekh toshnit — “We’re All Sick to Our Stomachs.” A few people held Yabloko flyers, but no one was handing them out in large numbers; party representatives directed supporters to pick up campaign materials at Yabloko’s headquarters on Pyatnitskaya Street.
“Anything besides flyers?” a boy of about 16 asked.
“No, just flyers.”
Every so often, a teenager the crowd had nicknamed the “Yabloko cosplayer” jogged along the sidewalk in a homemade red cap with a green leaf sticking out of the crown, resembling the party’s logo. In his hands was a big white Yabloko flag, furled around its pole. People kept asking him to unfurl it for photos; he obliged every time, then rolled it straight back up.
Volunteers with big bags worked through the crowd, offering apples, candy, cookies, and water, and collecting litter — there wasn’t a single trash can near the courthouse.
People everywhere were talking about how the hearing might end and which strategy would serve the opposition best in this campaign. Some criticized Yulia Navalnaya, who had publicly called on Russians to vote for Yabloko.
“They should have waited until three days before the vote!” a young man in light-colored pants told a friend heatedly.
“And how is everyone supposed to find out who to vote for [in that little time]?”
“People already know.”
“Some people don’t.”
”Four percent know!”
Meanwhile, inside the courtroom, Rybakov was speaking. The 47-year-old party chairman opened with memories of his school days in Leningrad and of teachers, many of whom had fought at the front or lived through the siege of the city:
From childhood I was taught: anything, so long as there’s no war. And they said it not only on May 9, [Victory Day]. If anyone had told them they were violating the copyright of our fellow Leningrader Alexander Moiseyevich Volodin, they, as front-line veterans, would have told that person exactly what they thought of him.
Rybakov told the court that the Central Election Commission had found no violations in Yabloko’s paperwork and had voted unanimously to register the party for the election. He said the Justice Ministry reviews the party’s reports regularly and has never found fault with them.
“The plaintiff has confused the Supreme Court with a political talk show,” Rybakov went on, in a reference to the regular appearances that Rodina’s leader, Alexey Zhuravlev, makes on state television to deliver propaganda talking points. “They have brought the court evidence that does not exist, that is [only] passed off as evidence: in fact it is personal fabrications, or quotations pulled out of context, and at times simply absurd notions.”
Rybakov spoke for 20 minutes. In that time, he took apart several of Rodina’s accusations, tried to draw the court’s attention to the incompetence of the plaintiff’s representatives (Judge Vyacheslav Kirillov cut him off), quoted Vladimir Putin (who has himself allowed for the possibility of peace talks), and read excerpts from voters’ letters.
The speech energized the people watching the feed outside. Many thought Rodina’s accusations were so ridiculous that the judge could not possibly heed them, and that Yabloko would therefore stay on the ballot. They had doubts about whether the opposition would actually win seats in the State Duma.
“No, they won’t get in — that won’t be allowed,” a curly-haired young man dressed all in black told Bereg. “The results will be handed down from above regardless.”
Asked why he still thought it mattered to back Yabloko in particular, he said it was a matter of principle to seize the moment — the first time in years that an opposition candidate would appear on the ballot. “The point is for people to know, for themselves, that they voted [with a clear conscience],” he said.
Another young man told Bereg that, all else being equal, he wouldn’t support Yabloko: he considers it “too left-wing,” and he called its platform one-sided — it says nothing, for instance, about a vision for the Russian economy. But all the other candidates, he said, are worse, because they back Putin and United Russia right down the line:
In a real democracy, I’d be fighting against Yabloko, but right now it’s the only one that connects us to Europe, which promises us freedom of speech. If even a couple of Yabloko deputies get in, that would be a win and a half.
Besides the young people in Yabloko or pacifist gear and the uniformed security officers, the plainclothes eshniki caught the eye — officers from Center E, the Interior Ministry’s anti-extremism directorate. Most tried not to draw attention to themselves, watching from across the street and filming Yabloko’s supporters from a distance. One of them — in sunglasses, a surgical mask, jeans, and a denim shirt — worked his way back and forth through the crowd, pulling out his phone now and then. He was the only person near the courthouse hiding his face.
A young man who was sketching noticed the masked eshnik. He pulled out a postcard with Yabloko’s logo on it and started drawing the officer’s portrait. The officer noticed him too, walked over, and began filming him from inches away on a smartphone. The artist wasn’t rattled. He kept working, showed the eshnik the finished sketch, and walked off. The mask made the officer’s reaction impossible to read.
By the end of the fourth hour of the hearing, only a handful of people were still following the proceedings: Yabloko’s and Rodina’s representatives kept going over the same fine points, and watching them was exhausting. The crowd had thinned since morning, too — some left for good, others stepped out for lunch and planned to come back. At 2:30 p.m., the judge called a half-hour recess, and everyone who hadn’t gone far hurried back to the building in case Rybakov came out to the supporters. Only Yabloko’s lawyers emerged.
Only those who had picked up a pass that morning were let back in, though plenty of seats were still empty.
“Never mind — we’ll be here to meet him,” an elderly woman said with a sigh on her way out through the checkpoint.
People kept hoping anyway, and a small line formed at the doors. Those waiting introduced themselves to one another, traded Telegram handles, and compared notes on what they had seen and heard.
“When Rybakov showed up — that was a show! Same vibe as when Messi came out for Inter Miami!”
“His media persona is always so calm. He’s like a good university lecturer.”
“The feed is unwatchable — they’re probably still on Hiroshima in there.”
Every so often, shouts and a recording of the chorus of “Yabloko” rang out from one part of the crowd or another — a song by Yolka and IOWA that has become the unofficial anthem of the party’s campaign. Gen Zers happily filmed TikToks to it.
A few young people circled the streets around the courthouse in a white car, waving campaign flyers out the windows with the same song blasting inside. They got bolder and started waving a big Yabloko flag out the window, and this time the police had had enough: a patrol car gave chase. The driver was fined 800 rubles (about $10) — not for disturbing the peace, but for driving without his vehicle registration.
“Russia will be fre—” someone in the crowd began chanting loudly, but was cut off.
“Quiet, quiet, don’t!” a man hissed, with a sideways glance at the police.
The self-censorship frustrated Mira, a Moscow resident whose name has been changed. She said she tries not to miss protests or high-profile trials, and that with so few such gatherings left, it matters to take the chance. She liked that the people who came were behaving so civilly. She was also coming around to the view that nothing in the country can be changed this way:
I was raised in a liberal system to believe in peaceful protest, clean hands [not stained with blood]. And where has that gotten us? To sitting here waiting for them to let Yabloko run.
Muscovites like Mira, with a history of activism, were scarce outside the court. For many of the people Bereg spoke with, all of this was new — and in September, they will make their first trip to a polling station.
“By the time I was 10, Putin had already been in power almost 20 years, and even then I understood it wasn’t normal. In other countries, [leaders] change every four years,” said a young man in a light blue polo shirt. “That’s when I started working on my United Russia relatives to vote [for someone else].”
There were plenty of very young activists outside the court as well — some just out of school, some still in it, all of them too young to vote.
“I worked on my grandmother for ages [not to vote for United Russia], and I barely managed it,” Nika (name changed) said, smiling. “She says, ‘Fine, I’ll vote for your apples.’”
Nika was among the first to arrive; at that point, she said, only a couple dozen people had gathered. She spent a long time choosing what to wear — she considered a hoodie with a big peace sign and a sweater reading “Navalny,” but thought better of drawing extra attention and limited her antiwar symbolism to a small peace-sign pendant.
Outside the court, Nika met Olya (name changed). Olya isn’t 18 yet either, and this was her first time at anything like it, but she had decided to come out for Yabloko almost by accident.
“I saw on Telegram that there was a Gen Z protest outside the courthouse, so I decided to head over,” Olya said. She had come in from the Moscow region, worried that everyone would be gone by evening — but several hundred people were still outside the Supreme Court. She reacted with excitement to everything going on outside and tried to keep up with the news from inside.
She looked completely happy. When she noticed a journalist filming her, though, she asked that no photo or video be published anywhere: “Otherwise … I’ll be in trouble with my family,” she said. Olya said she and her parents hold the same political views, but they would not be pleased to see her turn up at a protest.
A commotion started at the courthouse entrance, and Nika and Olya hurried over to see. Some young people were shooting a video in support of Yabloko: they had unfurled a party flag and an enormous Russian tricolor, and they were chanting “Russia!” at full volume. The police tensed a little but didn’t intervene. A minute later the chant changed, and the crowd was shouting “Yabloko!”
A large man in a blue suit came out of the courthouse, looked with distaste at the crowd of shouting, jumping teenagers, and waved over one of the officers.
“Could you keep it down? There are offices in here,” he complained.
“You’re going to wait somewhere else now,” the officer said, passing the request along to the crowd in the voice of a stern schoolteacher. “People are working here, and you’re shouting.”
The activists rolled up their flags and drifted apart a little, and the officer went back to his car. Now in the eighth hour of waiting, the crowd found new ways to kill time. Some inflated a big red balloon, covered it in Yabloko campaign slogans, and started a volleyball game. Others took chalk to the sidewalk in front of the entrance, and party logos and the words “For Yabloko,” “For peace,” and “For freedom” spread across the pavement.
The police didn’t like that either. They demanded an end to the performances and pulled several people aside to take down their personal information. Nobody was detained.
Passersby reacted to the crowd in different ways. Some were annoyed that the supporters had filled the entire sidewalk, forcing people to squeeze past. Others smiled and gave a barely perceptible nod when they caught an activist’s eye. A few showed their support outright.
“Am I right that the Yabloko hearing is here today?” a young bearded man asked.
“Yes, that’s right.”
“Good for them! I should have come too,” he said, raising his fist in approval — and walked on without joining.
In the ninth hour of the hearing, Judge Kirillov finally retired to deliberate. Several hundred people began lining up around the entrance to be among the first to greet Rybakov, and every conversation in the crowd came back to the trial and the feelings it had stirred.
“I haven’t been this nervous since I broke up with my girlfriend!”
“I don’t get why Rodina didn’t withdraw a single accusation — every one of them was refuted.”
“There’s this euphoria, you can feel it, right?”
With every minute the crowd pressed tighter around the entrance, and the street beside the court filled with more security officers — in balaclavas and helmets now — and more official cars. Some in the crowd grew nervous.
“If a … commotion starts, you’ll never get out of this crowd,” a man’s voice said.
At some point, people started singing — not Monetochka or Noize MC, but classics from Soviet cartoons: first “A Ray of Golden Sunshine,” then “The Song of the Bremen Town Musicians.” The third song was “Changes” by the band Kino, and the security officers, more or less calm until then, tensed up: the patrol cars let out a low-frequency drone to tell the singers it was time to stop.
The crowd went quiet for a moment, then someone started chanting “Yabloko.” One of the officers took out a megaphone and called for order, menacingly. People complied.
The pause didn’t last. A woman’s voice struck up “Along the Path of Good,” from the Soviet film The Adventures of Little Mook. The crowd picked it up fast, though some of the activists self-censored again.
“Guys, let’s not sing!” a nervous voice called out.
“So we just stand here? Then what’s the point of this protest?”
Judge Kirillov took more than an hour to decide. The moment the feed came back, everyone froze, eyes on their phone screens. When they heard that Yabloko had indeed been removed from the ballot, an angry rumble went through the crowd, and almost at once people started shouting: “Shame!”
The police had had enough. They quickly sealed the street beside the courthouse with an enormous National Guard prisoner transport van and patrol cars; officers in balaclavas lined up along the curb; riot police blocked the sidewalk.
“Five minutes, and you’ll get what you wanted,” one of the officers shouted furiously into a megaphone — not a promise that Rybakov was about to come out, but a threat of rough detentions. He demanded that people clear the area around the court as fast as possible.
The crowd churned, and some people tried to break away and run. One after another, the spectators who had made it into the hearing that morning came out of the building and looked at the chaos by the steps, uncomprehending. Some of the women had been crying.
Seeing that some people refused to go, the officer returned to threats.
“You have two or three minutes, and if you don’t disperse, don’t come complaining,” he said into the megaphone, calmer now but still angry. “Nobody’s going to come get you out of the enlistment office, young men. I’ve warned you.”
At last Rybakov came out of the building with his team. The crowd met him with applause and cheers, then started chanting “Yabloko!” and “Well done!”
Turning a green apple over in his hands, Rybakov smiled sadly and thanked the crowd for its support. He urged supporters not to lose heart, as Yabloko still had five days to appeal the Supreme Court’s ruling:
For very many of you, everything is only just beginning today. You came to us for the first time — we’ve only just gotten to know each other. We have a long, shared road ahead of us. And we have a very big and important task: together, to stop the deaths, to bring back peace, to save human lives.
The supporters applauded again and chanted “Thank you!” With every second, the mood grew more anxious. Would the security forces make good on their threats, with this many journalists present and the leader of a registered political party standing in the middle of it?
“Nikolai, they’re going to round us up!” a young voice shouted.
“Yeah, somebody get us out of here,” another said.
“Here’s what we do: we disperse carefully now,” Rybakov said. “Nobody shouts anything — [then] nobody should get rounded up, I very much [hope]. But leave one at a time, so it isn’t a march, so they can’t call it a provocation.”
Supporters gathered around Rybakov for selfies and goodbye hugs. Waiting their turn to leave Povarskaya Street, people talked about whom to vote for if Yabloko failed to overturn the ruling on appeal.
“The Greens, maybe?”
“They’re pro-war too.”
“New People are pro-war as well — they passed all those [repressive] bills.”
“What about Democratic Initiative, or whatever it’s called? Something with ‘direct democracy’ in it.”
“Honestly, I have no idea what that is.”
A woman of about 50 joined the young people’s conversation. She said that she and other opposition supporters who had “been following [politics] a long time” had no illusions that Yabloko would be left on the ballot, but that she came to the courthouse anyway, for “a few hours of freedom.”
“I turn 18 on the 19th, as it happens,” a young man told her, smiling shyly.
“So you’ll be able to come on the 20th?” [Voting runs September 18–20, with the main day on the 20th.]
“Yes, of course I’ll go. I just need to listen to Ekaterina Mikhailovna [Schulmann] first.”
“And Yulia [Navalnaya] too.”
“Yes, and Yulia, of course!”
The officer switched on his megaphone again.
“Citizens! The hearing is over, please vacate … the sidewalk,” he said, stumbling as he realized how absurd his demand was. “Keep moving toward the subway, don’t linger.”
Seeing that people were in no hurry to leave, Rybakov volunteered to walk them to the subway himself. He led them toward the station, keeping an eye out for anyone having trouble with the security officers. Along the way he kept taking selfies, joking, and answering questions — even personal ones, like which station he lives near. When someone suggested he join them for dinner at McDonald’s, he politely declined.
The line “He’s just like Lyosha!” — [a diminutive for Alexey Navalny] — rippled through the crowd.
The security officers escorted the group all the way to the subway. At the entrance, Rybakov thanked his supporters once more, and they responded with applause. The crowd then dispersed into the station.

'It won't fall apart': Leading Liberal says we don't need 'gold-plated' building code
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:55:14 UTC
03:55:14 KST

From a tome to a pamphlet: Liberal Andrew Bragg vows to demolish building code
In short:
Opposition housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg has promised to slash the National Construction Code from over 2,000 pages to 80 if elected.
Building groups and the Productivity Commission have estimated that regulations add thousands to the cost of each newly built home.
What's next?
Much of the construction code deals with inconsistencies across states and territories, which the federal government does not have the power to change.
The federal opposition wants to demolish Australia's building code, squeezing more than 2,000 pages into just 80.
Speaking at the National Press Club on Wednesday, Liberal housing spokesman Andrew Bragg will say the current rules require "gold-plated houses", which are too expensive.
In a radical overhaul which would require the co-operation of states and territories to deliver, he would turn everything apart from basic safety standards into an "optional extra", including accessibility and energy efficiency requirements.
"It is now illegal to build a cheap house in Australia," the senator will say, according to excerpts from his remarks shared with the ABC.
"We will pare this back."
The National Construction Code, established under a different name in 1988, was initially in the order of eighty pages but has expanded under successive governments.
While some of this is due to expanding scope, the document has also evolved to give builders more detailed guidance on how they can ensure their buildings are compliant.
Another major cause of bloat is the section devoted to explaining variations across each state and territory.
That alone spans more than 700 pages across multiple volumes, resulting in what the Productivity Commission calls a "thicket" of inconsistency.
Regulations add thousands to the cost of a house
Industry groups argue complicated regulations add to the cost of new homes.
Evidence heard by a Senate inquiry into productivity, which Senator Bragg chaired, found the last seven years of code changes have added $3,600 to $33,000 to the cost of a new house.
A recent Productivity Commission inquiry into the construction sector found that zoning and the regulatory approvals process was more burdensome than building regulations, but its terms of reference did not include direct consideration of the construction code.
While Senator Bragg's proposal would see much of the existing guidance retained as "optional" and the desired length is informed by New Zealand's approach, such a dramatic reduction could involve risks.
For example, while Senator Bragg has suggested that "essential structural, fire safety, and health-related" standards will be retained, the fire-related sections alone in the existing code run to more than 80 pages.
Senator Bragg's speech suggests houses under the shorter code "won't be gold plated but it won't fall apart. It will be safe."
The proposed new code would be accompanied by a federal "pattern book" with approved templates.
While the code is developed nationally by the Australian Building Codes Board (ABCB), it is implemented in state and territory laws, meaning any changes would require co-operation across jurisdictions.
Expanding scope over time
The total page figure of just over 2,200 pages includes all kinds of buildings, not just homes.
ABCB chief executive Adrian Piani told Senator Bragg's inquiry the section relating to "your standard house" was just 332 pages.
Mr Piani said there were two main reasons the code had expanded. One was the inclusion of guidance.
"It became much more of a document that was trying to give people the answer as well as the performance requirement," he said.
"[The earlier version says] if it's got stairs, those stairs must help people leave the building … [The later version] has all the pictures, all the diagrams about how you design a stair and what a stair looks like."
But the other reason was expanded scope. Recent changes include a mandated seven-star energy efficiency rating and mandatory accessibility standards.
Senator Bragg listed "mandatory ramps" and "flattened shower flooring" as examples.
The federal government announced a freeze to the code last year, but has since indicated it is taking steps to simplify it in co-ordination with the building industry.
Treasury's Inspector-General of Housing, Ben Rimmer, told Senate estimates earlier this year the complexity of the construction code was "a significant impost on the economy" and a "significant driver of cost", but that much of this was due to states and territories.
"We don't have a National Construction Code … we actually have eight different construction regulatory systems depending on which state and territory you happen to be in on that day of the week," he said.
"If you're a plumber living in Wodonga and you cross the border, you have a different set of regulations … We're working to improve it and to make sure that we get a better system as soon as we can within those constraints."
In the same estimates hearing, Labor minister Tim Ayres criticised Senator Bragg's longstanding aspiration to slash the code, noting that recent changes included measures to improve waterproofing for balconies.
"I just don't think you can argue — well, you can if you want — [against] stopping people having to spend $2 billion in rectification costs because apartment balconies are leaking," he said.
"I just think that's a sensible proposition … leaking balconies are a bad idea."
Speech to canvas migration
Senator Bragg will also argue the Albanese government has allowed net overseas migration to outpace housing construction, creating a shortfall of 130,000 homes.
The Coalition intends to link migration to housing completions.
"This … can be achieved while benefiting the budget and the economy, including by lifting the skilled share of our permanent migration … and modest reductions in international students, working holiday makers and post-study work visas."
Labor is preparing its own plan to keep net migration closer to Treasury projections, as reported by the ABC last week.
The details have been the subject of extensive cabinet debate, and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said on Monday there was "work to do".
A National Press Club address by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, cancelled at short notice last week, has not yet been scheduled but is expected as soon as next week.
Labor's proposal is expected to include restrictions on working holiday makers and those who fail in their applications for humanitarian visas, including many graduated students.
Plans for skilled migrants and their families are unclear.

What to know about Wednesday's total solar eclipse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
18:51:30 UTC
03:51:30 KST

2026's only total solar eclipse happens tomorrow. Here's the path and times of visibility.
The only total solar eclipse of 2026 will have people looking to the skies as darkness falls on its path across part of the Northern Hemisphere on Wednesday.
First, if you've never had the opportunity to see a solar eclipse, what you are watching is the moon passing in front of the sun. It occurs somewhere on Earth about every 18 months, but in any one particular spot on the globe they could happen hundreds of years apart.
Here's what to know about when and where to see the total solar eclipse:
Where will the solar eclipse be visible?
Many of the best places to view totality are not inhabited, like northern Greenland. But western Iceland and northern Spain are also on the path of totality for a peak eclipse experience.
In Spain, they have not experienced a total solar eclipse since 1905.
This animation from NASA shows the path of totality for the eclipse, along with the time when it will cross those areas:
Even though totality will be visible in only a few populated regions, a partial solar eclipse will be visible in a much wider area. About 230 million people will be able to see 90% totality, according to population data from the Center for International Earth Science Information Network at Columbia University.
Most major cities in Europe will see at least 90% totality, including Madrid, London and Paris.
Even some of North America will get a chance to see a partial solar eclipse, though it won't be nearly as impressive as when the U.S. got to see a total eclipse in 2024. The best place to see it in the U.S. is in Fairbanks, Alaska, where it will reach 37% totality.
Boston will see 16% totality, while New York City will see about 9% totality, Toronto will see about 8% and Philadelphia will see 7%.
What time will the eclipse happen?
Since the eclipse is crossing just the northern part of the globe, the path of totality will be fairly short from start to finish, about an hour and 45 minutes.
The total eclipse will first become visible in extreme northern Russia at 17:00 UTC, which is 1 p.m. Eastern time.
It will reach northeast Greenland by 1:30 p.m. ET and western Iceland by about 1:45 p.m. ET (totality will be at exactly 5:48 p.m. local time in Reykjavík).
After crossing the northern Atlantic for 45 minutes — when it will be best visible in the U.K., with London reaching its max of 91% at 2:13 p.m. ET (7:13 p.m. local time) — totality will reach northern Spain at about 2:30 p.m. ET (exactly 8:32 p.m. local time in Valencia).
The whole path will be over by 2:45 p.m. ET.
For those in North America seeing a partial eclipse, it will be most full in Toronto at 1:40 p.m. and New York City at 1:54 p.m. local time. In Fairbanks, you will need to get up early to see its fullest point at 8:27 a.m. local time.
How do I watch the eclipse in person?
If you are lucky enough to be in one of the locations where the solar eclipse reaches totality, it will last for about two minutes.
You will need to wear solar eclipse glasses to safely view the sun during the event to protect your retinas from damage. You can take your glasses off for that two minutes when it's at totality.
If you're outside the path of totality but lucky enough to at least get a partial eclipse, you'll have to leave those glasses on the whole time to avoid eye damage.
When is the next total solar eclipse in the U.S.?
If hearing about the total solar eclipse in Europe gets you excited for the next one in the U.S., you have some time to wait.
The next total solar eclipse over the U.S. will be in 2044, but that one will only be visible in three states: Montana, North Dakota and South Dakota.
The next year, there will be another opportunity visible in many states as it moves from coast to coast. The eclipse will start in Northern California and move in an arc towards the east, ending in Florida, similar to one in 2017. There will be numerous U.S. cities where eclipse watchers can view the total eclipse, including Reno, Nevada; Colorado Springs; Tulsa, Oklahoma; Little Rock, Arkansas; Jackson, Mississippi; and Orlando, Florida.
There will be another in 2052 that crosses the Southeast, including Florida, Georgia and South Carolina.
To see a total eclipse in the northeastern U.S., you'll have to wait all the way until May 1, 2079.
How to watch coverage of the 2026 total solar eclipse
- What: Total solar eclipse across parts of the Northern Hemisphere
- Date: Aug. 12, 2026
- Time: Live coverage begins at 2 p.m. ET
- Location: The path of totality stretches from extreme northern Russia across parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain. Most major cities in Europe will see at least 90% totality, including Madrid, London and Paris. CBS News live streaming coverage will feature Rob Marciano in Mallorca, Spain, where totality hits at about 2:30 p.m. ET.
- Online stream: Live on CBS News in the video player above and on your mobile or streaming device
