US human rights groups sue Trump over anti-ICC push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:34:36 UTC
23:34:36 KST

US human rights groups sue Trump over anti-ICC push
- Four US human rights groups sued the Trump administration for unconstitutional sanctions against ICC officials aiming to block justice for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
- Trump's 2025 executive order targets ICC staff for prosecuting US and Israeli officials, with the administration campaigning globally to undermine the court.
- The lawsuit follows similar legal challenges and criticism that the ICC threatens US sovereignty, with Trump stating the push defends Israel's leaders, not himself.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Four leading US human rights groups on Aug 11 sued the Trump administration over its campaign aimed at dismantling the International Criminal Court (ICC), calling the effort unconstitutional.
US President Donald Trump in 2025 issued an executive order authorising sanctions on prosecutors, judges and others working with the court for pursuing cases against officials from the US and its ally Israel, neither of which are members of the ICC.
Human Rights Watch, the Open Society Institute, the American Friends Service Committee and the Center for Constitutional Rights said in their lawsuit filed in New York that those sanctions prevent them from working with the court to seek justice for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity around the world.
“The plaintiffs are seeking an end to this sanctions regime, which transgresses the President’s authority and violates international and US law, including the rights to freedom of expression and religion,” lead counsel Andrew Loewenstein of Foley Hoag, which is representing the human rights groups, said in a statement.
The lawsuit comes after a similar one filed in July by advocacy groups who work on human rights for Palestinians. In response to that lawsuit, the State Department said the groups were seeking to “enable ICC overreach” and said the court posed a threat to US sovereignty.
Three ICC judges have separately sued the Trump administration over the sanctions.
Trump’s opposition towards the ICC goes back to his first term. A similar executive order Trump issued in 2020 was blocked by a judge, who said it likely violated the First Amendment, before being rescinded by President Joe Biden’s administration in 2021.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in July that the administration would step up efforts to undermine the court in The Hague, including with a diplomatic campaign aimed at persuading other countries to quit it. Rubio argued that the court posed a threat to US personnel carrying out Trump’s hard-line immigration policies or strikes on boats accused of carrying drugs, as well as other US service members.
Trump, during a July 31 Cabinet meeting, said in response to an update from Rubio that the campaign was aimed at defending Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and others, rather than Trump himself. REUTERS

Too hot to live? French buyers rethink housing choices after heatwaves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:34:00 UTC
23:34:00 KST

Too hot to live? French buyers rethink housing choices after heatwaves
- French homebuyers now prioritise cooling features like shutters, air-conditioning, and indirect sunlight due to frequent severe heatwaves.
- Many properties, especially top-floor Paris apartments, become unbearable in heat, leading buyers to reconsider orientation and ventilation.
- While no mass relocation occurs yet, climate comfort is becoming a key factor in housing decisions amid growing climate risks.
AI generated
PARIS – After multiple severe heatwaves in a single summer, French residents are increasingly factoring high temperatures into their home hunts, realtors say, bumping up features such as shutters, air-conditioning and indirect sunlight on their priority lists.
In Paris, in particular the summer of 2026, the steep temperatures turned apartments directly under iconic Haussmann-era buildings with zinc-covered roofs into virtual ovens.
“On the top floor of a Haussmann-style building, the heat indoors can become truly unbearable,” said Joseph Denke, an estate agent with FredeLion in Paris.
He has noted a shift in buyers’ priorities in recent months, including being wary of south-facing windows.
The heat risk in a studio apartment under the eaves with no through air – windows on just one side for example – was a negative point for Camille Couturier during a viewing with Denke.
“We’re seeing that heatwaves are happening in June, or even May,” the 30-year-old said.
For his future flat, he is thinking “at least 10 to 15 years ahead” and is concerned about whether he will be able to “live comfortably in it” or end up “having to flee like everyone else because it’s too hot”.
According to a study by Pouget Consultants and IGNES, one in two homes in France is effectively a heat trap.
Among 1,750 users of the classified ads platform Leboncoin surveyed in June, eight out of 10 said they had experienced discomfort during periods of extreme heat, with a third saying they would consider moving if heatwaves became more intense.
Experts have warned that due to climate change, this is to be expected. France’s national weather agency said on Aug 10 as France braced itself for its fifth heatwave of the season that “future summers will generally be hotter than those experienced to date”.
For Leboncoin’s marketing director Sophie Bourg, heatwaves are now “firmly recognised as a structural factor in housing choices” in France.
“Coolness and summer comfort have become a property criterion in their own right,” she said.
Shutters and trees
Orientation, floor level, swimming pools, air conditioning, shutters, the ability to create through-draughts, outdoor space, shaded terraces and even the presence of trees in a neighbourhood are now among the issues increasingly raised by buyers or tenants.
“Buyers are no longer looking only at the property itself, but at how liveable it is,” said Yann Jehanno, president of the Laforet estate agency network.
“They are asking estate agents very practical questions about temperatures during the last heatwave, whether it is possible to ventilate the home at night, and whether people sleep well in the bedrooms,” he said.
The concern is already affecting the appeal of certain properties.
Christian Tokoto, an estate agent with Guy Hoquet Paris 5 Maubert, is trying to sell “a magnificent apartment with large windows” in Paris’ well-heeled fifth district.
“Despite lots of viewings, clients tell us it’s ‘too hot’ because it doesn’t have windows on both sides. So for now it’s still on the market,” he said.
Air-conditioning, long disdained in France, is “no longer taboo at all”, Jehanno said.
It is “a huge selling point for many buyers” if it is already installed, especially in blocks where getting permission for an AC unit can be complicated, said Laetitia Caron, chief executive of real estate media company PAP.
Sellers have adapted accordingly, she added, placing greater emphasis in listings on features linked to summer comfort such as air-conditioning and shutters.
No exodus yet
The impact of recent heatwaves on where people choose to live is harder to assess.
“We are not seeing an exodus yet,” Bourg said.
But whereas people once chose a location primarily for its attractiveness and the opportunities it offered, they are now also making decisions based on “climatic comfort”, something she describes as entirely new.
Jehanno believes these trends reflect a lasting change in attitudes.
There is “clearly an impact from climate change on the property market”, he said, pointing to challenges such as heatwaves, wildfires and other weather extremes.
Such risks, he said, make it increasingly difficult for buyers “to plan ahead over the 10 to 20 years of a mortgage”. AFP

In France, three nuclear reactors were shut down due to an influx of jellyfish

In France, three nuclear reactors were shut down due to an influx of jellyfish
Kyiv • UNN
In Gravelines, France, three nuclear reactors were shut down due to an influx of jellyfish, while another is operating with restrictions. Operator EDF reported that the animals are interfering with operations, but there is no threat to safety.
In Gravelines, France, on the English Channel coast, an influx of jellyfish forced three nuclear power plant reactors to be shut down at once. Another is operating with restrictions. The plant operator, EDF, said that the animals were interfering with operations—the nuclear power plant requires clean water, UNN reports, citing Bild.
Details
This is not the first time jellyfish have caused problems for the nuclear power plant. Last year, they were already entering the filters of the water-pumping systems en masse. The reactors then also had to be disconnected from the grid for several days. EDF did not report exactly how the animals are causing problems this time. According to the operator, there are no consequences for the safety of the power plant, its employees, or the environment.
Jellyfish stopped four reactors of France's largest nuclear power plant12.08.25, 05:08 • 4523 views
We would add
The Gravelines nuclear power plant is located between Calais and Dunkirk on France’s northern coast. It has six reactors and is considered one of France’s most important nuclear facilities.

Turkey may propose creating two security corridors in Black Sea — paper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:32:43 UTC
23:32:43 KST

ISTANBUL, August 11. /TASS/. Turkey may put forward an initiative to set up two security corridors in the Black Sea - one for ships bound for Russia and another for ones heading to Ukraine, while a no-attack rule would be attached, pro-government newspaper Yeni Safak said.
Yeni Safak also points out that Turkey may restrict fishing by local fishermen outside the country's territorial waters in the Black Sea.
Ankara has not yet commented on the report. A local business source told TASS that information about the creation of safety corridors fits well into the authorities' plans to ensure the safety of navigation.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan previously said that Ankara is closely monitoring the safety of navigation in the Black Sea and has conveyed to the parties to the Ukrainian conflict a proposal for a moratorium on military action.
The Dunya newspaper said that the association of Turkish shipowners and operators of coastal navigation invited Ankara and international organizations to sit down at the negotiating table to establish a new offshore grain corridor like the previously created one under the Black Sea grain initiative. It believes that this has become an urgent need both for regional trade and for ensuring global food security.
The grain deal was signed in Istanbul in 2022 to ensure a safe sea corridor for the produce exports from the Black Sea ports and terminated next year. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly pointed out that the West exported most of the Ukrainian grain to their countries, while the main purpose of the deal - supplies to the countries in need, including those in Africa - was never realized.

Pakistan says US, Iran nearing deal as Hormuz tensions persist and oil prices fall

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:32:14 UTC
23:32:14 KST

Pakistan’s defense minister said Tuesday that the United States and Iran appeared to be nearing an agreement, offering a rare sign of progress in negotiations even as Washington and Tehran continued to trade threats and U.S. forces enforced a blockade of Iranian ports.
Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif told Bloomberg that developments over the past several days suggested the two sides were moving closer to "some sort of an arrangement."
“Things are shaping up again in favor of a peace arrangement or a deal,” Asif said. “The signals in the last two, three days are that we are close to some sort of an arrangement.”
Oil prices fell following Asif’s comments amid renewed hopes for an agreement, Bloomberg reported. The remarks came alongside reports that Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had arrived in Tehran for talks.
Until now, negotiations had appeared to be stalled.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who said Monday that he was “low keying” on Iran, later renewed his threats against Tehran in a Truth Social post.
“I see that Representatives of the Islamic Republic of Iran are asking for compensation for the damage done to them during the last five month Military Conflict,” Trump wrote. “[I]t is an interesting idea because now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by General Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat.”
Later, speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump was asked what he would do if the latest round of negotiations failed to produce an agreement and whether a broader escalation of the fighting remained an option.
“We have that certainly in that ability if we want to do that,” Trump said.
The diplomatic maneuvering came as U.S. forces reportedly attacked a Panama-flagged ship Tuesday morning as it attempted to evade the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports.
The Wall Street Journal reported that a U.S. military helicopter fired a Hellfire missile at the ship's rudder after its crew ignored warnings from American forces enforcing the blockade, citing a U.S. official.
There were no immediate reports of injuries in the incident, which occurred before dawn. The U.S. official said the vessel appeared to have attempted to transfer its crew to another civilian ship following the attack.
A maritime security company separately reported that a Panama-flagged container ship identified as the Vela Nova had been struck by a missile fired from a helicopter as it sailed west through the Gulf of Oman, about 131 kilometers (81 miles) off the coast of Pakistan.
“The missile struck the vessel and caused a fire, which was subsequently extinguished,” the security company said in an initial report.
All 17 crew members were unharmed, according to the company.
The incident underscored the continuing military tensions surrounding the negotiations. The United States has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports that has constrained Tehran’s ability to export oil, adding to economic pressure on the Islamic Republic.
Israel, meanwhile, is closely following reports from Washington that Trump could seek to declare victory and bring the war with Iran to an end even without an agreement dismantling Tehran’s nuclear program, provided Iran agrees to reopen the Strait of Hormuz without restrictions.
The strait, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea, is one of the world’s most important energy corridors and a critical route for global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.
Israeli officials have expressed concern about the possibility of an abrupt shift in Trump’s approach.
“There is an element of concern because Trump is unpredictable and also tends to change his mind,” an Israeli official said Monday.
The prevailing assessment in Israel is that Trump is reluctant to resume large-scale fighting but wants to maintain economic pressure on Iran, including through the blockade of its seaports and restrictions affecting its ability to export oil.
A senior Israeli official said the current situation was favorable to Israel because it maintained pressure on Tehran without requiring an immediate return to intensive fighting.
“The current situation is the best for us — the blockade remains in place and the economic pressure on Iran continues,” the official said.

Colombia earthquake: Rescuers race to find thousands missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:31:00 UTC
23:31:00 KST

Colombia earthquake: Rescuers race to find thousands missing
August 11, 2026
Rescuers and volunteers searched through collapsed buildings across western Colombia on Tuesday after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake caused widespread destruction across several major cities a day prior.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella said at least 181 people died in the quake, while around 2,595 people were injured.
While the president said around 195 people are missing, civilian-run databases indicate at least 3,900 people are still unaccounted for.
What do we know about the western Colombia earthquake?
The quake struck near the community of San Jose del Palmar in the western region of Choco on Monday, causing widespread destruction in the cities of Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo and Buenaventura.
Cali accounted for 85 deaths and Pereira 66, according to the association.
The figures remain incomplete because they largely cover major cities and do not yet include the full toll from rural communities.
Thousands have been reporting missing, with many feared trapped beneath collapsed buildings.
Around 1,600 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. Soldiers, emergency teams and relatives have been clearing debris in dozens of towns and cities, with volunteers forming lines to pass chunks of concrete by hand.
The cities of Pereira, Cali, Quibdo and Manizales remain on red alert because of the scale of the damage.
At least 165 buildings completely collapsed in those cities alone. Hospitals, airports, public utilities and transport systems have also been damaged across several western departments.
The epicenter was near one of Colombia's poorest and most isolated regions. Large parts of the area can be reached only by boat, aircraft or through jungle routes, while damaged roads and other infrastructure are complicating access. That means the full extent of casualties and destruction near the epicenter remains unclear.
How has the world responded?
The United States has offered $15.5 million (€13.42 million) in emergency assistance, while the European Union has activated its Copernicus satellite service to support rescue operations.
The EU has also begun providing emergency assistance following the earthquake, including €100,000 in initial aid through the German Red Cross.
Israel, Mexico, Chile, Argentina and El Salvador have also offered assistance.
The earthquake was felt beyond Colombia, including in parts of Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama.
Why was such a deep quake so damaging?
The scale of the destruction was striking because the earthquake struck at a depth of around 100 kilometers (62 miles), where surface shaking would normally be expected to be weaker.
Geologist Raul Perez of Spain's Geological and Mining Institute told EFE news agency that the magnitude 7.4 quake was a particularly complex subduction event involving the Nazca and South American tectonic plates.
He said a "site effect" in some areas amplified the seismic waves as they passed through local geological formations, increasing both the strength and duration of the shaking and worsening damage to buildings.
Perez said the combination of the quake's unusual depth, its magnitude and the local amplification effects made it an event that would need to be studied closely.

Mass graves found after Sudan army recaptures Kurmuk from RSF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:28:32 UTC
23:28:32 KST

Breadcrumb
Mass graves found after Sudan army recaptures Kurmuk from RSF
More than a month after Sudanese troops recaptured the strategic border town of Kurmuk, authorities searching an area northeast of the town say they have found a grim remnant of the fighting - mass graves containing the bodies of 25 civilians.
The dead included women, children and health workers, according to Abdel Aty Mohamed al-Faki, the commissioner of Kurmuk in Sudan's Blue Nile state.
Al-Faki said the graves were discovered on Monday near Jebel Fankat during operations conducted after the Sudanese army retook the area from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its allies. He said that the victims had been executed by the RSF during its occupation of Kurmuk.
The New Arab could not independently verify the circumstances of the deaths or responsibility for the killings.
The discovery comes more than a month after the Sudanese army retook Kurmuk on 8 July following fighting with the RSF and the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) faction led by Abdelaziz al-Hilu.
The RSF and SPLM-N had seized Kurmuk on 24 March as part of an offensive across the Blue Nile region, opening a new front in Sudan's more than three-year war.
Jebel Fankat, where the graves were found, had been used by the RSF as a position for launching suicide drones during the battle for the town, according to al-Faki.
The reported presence of health workers among the bodies has also renewed attention on earlier allegations of attacks on medical facilities during the RSF's capture of Kurmuk.
In March, the Sudan Doctors Network accused RSF fighters of looting health facilities, destroying the town's main hospital and assaulting medical workers after entering Kurmuk.
The independent medical group said equipment and supplies were stolen and one health worker was critically injured, while thousands of residents fled the area. The RSF did not respond at the time to the network's allegations.
A new front in Sudan's war
Fighting in Blue Nile intensified earlier this year after the RSF formed a military alliance with al-Hilu's SPLM-N, pushing the war into territory along Sudan's borders with Ethiopia and South Sudan.
The alliance captured a string of towns and military positions before the army launched a counteroffensive, gradually advancing towards Kurmuk and retaking the town in July.
Kurmuk, close to the Ethiopian border, has long held strategic importance because of its position along cross-border routes. The town has repeatedly changed hands during Sudan's previous civil wars.
This year's fighting again sent tens of thousands of people fleeing Kurmuk and surrounding areas, placing further pressure on communities elsewhere in Blue Nile.
The graves reported this week are not the first to emerge from territory retaken during Sudan's war.
Bodies showing signs of execution have previously been found after government forces regained territory around Khartoum and Gezira, while rights groups and investigators have documented killings, torture and arbitrary detention by parties to the conflict.
Sudan's war began in April 2023 after the collapse of a power-sharing arrangement between army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo.
More than three years later, the conflict has spread across much of the country, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing millions. Both the RSF and forces aligned with the army have faced allegations of war crimes and other serious abuses.

Oil prices edged lower on Tuesday after reaching a more-than-one-week high, as analysts assessed signs of progress in talks between Oman and Iran regarding shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while disruptions to energy supplies from the Middle East continued. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
Brent crude futures fell 50 cents, or 0.57%, to $87.22 a barrel by 13:17 GMT. U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures declined 36 cents, or 0.44%, to $81.77 a barrel.
Both benchmark crude grades reached their highest levels since July 31 earlier in the session: Brent rose to $90.03 a barrel, while WTI reached $84.61.
Talks between Oman and Iran on the future of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz are currently at an advanced stage, a spokesperson for Qatar's Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday.
Any signs of de-escalation or a deal are good news for risk assets and, obviously, bad for oil. But for now, these are just talks. These are just headlines. There has been no significant progress
Both contracts jumped more than 5% on Monday after U.S. President Donald Trump responded to Iran's conditions for a peace deal with his own demands that Iran pay compensation for those killed in wars, attacks and protests, which is likely to complicate efforts to restore traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
I don't see oil prices falling below $80 in the near term unless there is an unexpected announcement of a deal that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, as the oil market is tightening
Addendum
Shipping data showed that traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to six vessels on Monday, compared with a 10-day average of about 11 vessels.
In a note on Monday, Barclays analysts said that net exports of crude oil and oil products through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 3 million barrels per day in the week ending August 7, compared with 4.4 million barrels per day the previous week.

Kuressaare Airport closure raises tourism concerns during August peak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:19:00 UTC
23:19:00 KST

Kuressaare Airport closure raises tourism concerns during August peak
Tour operators fear the closure of the airport linking Saaremaa to the mainland for the rest of August could impact negatively on visitor numbers, Maaleht reported.
Kuressaare Airport has flight routes not only to and from Tallinn but also outside Estonia, namely Helsinki.
Kuressaare Airport is closed to scheduled flights for three weeks from Monday, even as August is the second busiest month of the year after July, and considered the tail end of summer peak season.
Anu Lomp, head of tourism and marketing at Saaremaa's rural municipal government, said: "We very much hope that the lack of an air connection will not prevent people from coming to the island," though added some potential visitors had already been put off "as traveling by land is time-consuming."
"Of course, it is inconvenient that the airport is being closed from the beginning of August for most of the month, while the tourism season is still in full swing," she said, though it was understandable that the airport needed upgrading.
While the absolute number of air passengers is small compared with the overall number of people traveling between Saaremaa and the mainland, the economic impact per passenger can be significantly greater, particularly in the case of foreign visitors, Lomp added.
Lomp said the Tallinn-Kuressaare route has proved a pleasant surprise for many foreign visitors, noting the Helsinki-Kuressaare route has performed particularly well, carrying more than 2,300 passengers this year and with next year's flights already announced.
The Tallinn-Kuressaare air route is also important for local residents and business travelers who rely on its convenience and speed, particularly as from September there will no longer be a bus connection allowing people to reach Tallinn before 10 a.m. Maaleht reported.
Kuressaare Airport's runway will be closed for reconstruction from August 10–31, suspending scheduled flights, while rescue and medical helicopters can still function, said Tormi Loide, operations manager at Tallinn Airport, the Kuressaare airport's parent company.
The runway reconstruction was scheduled for August as Estonia's limited weather window for asphalt surfacing, markings and electrical work makes later months riskier, with September and October bringing a higher chance of delays and compromised quality, Maaleht said.
The upgrades will renew the runway's asphalt surface and markings, replace existing lights with energy-efficient LEDs, and install a Pilot Controlled Lighting (PCL) system enabling pilots to activate the airfield lights when needed.
The airport is scheduled to reopen to air traffic on September 1.

New Swissness rule runs into widespread opposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
14:18:00 UTC
23:18:00 KST

New Swissness rule runs into widespread opposition
A new regulation allows the Swiss cross to be used on goods manufactured abroad. According to two surveys, SMEs and voters are firmly opposed to the new regulation, the Swiss Trade Association told the media in Bern.
Both business owners and voters fear that this will dilute the “Switzerland” brand and lead to a loss of consumer confidence. The Swiss Trade Association commissioned two surveys on this issue, it said on Tuesday.
The non-representative online survey was aimed at cantonal associations and received 289 responses. In parallel, the Demoscope Institute carried out a representative survey of 1,154 voters between mid-July and early August.
The results of both surveys painted a consistent picture. Almost 90% of the tradespeople and eligible voters surveyed believed that the Swiss cross should remain the exclusive right of domestic producers.
In the Demoscope survey, 60% of respondents stated that their confidence in the significance of the Swiss cross was diminishing as a result of the change in practice. Half of the business owners rated the new regulation as “very detrimental” to SMEs without overseas manufacturing.
More
What does ‘Made in Switzerland’ mean exactly?
In both the business and public surveys, nearly nine out of ten respondents believed that the economy would be better supported if the Swiss cross remained the exclusive preserve of Swiss producers. A large majority also feared that a shift of production abroad would weaken Switzerland’s position as a centre of innovation.
This view was supported by Sven Reinecke, Executive Director of the Institute for Marketing & Customer Insight at the University of St Gallen (HSG). Images such as the Swiss cross have a more immediate impact than words and are perceived by consumers as a signal of origin and quality for the product as a whole, he said.
The association is therefore calling for the exclusivity of the Swiss cross for domestic producers to be reinstated swiftly, so as not to weaken Switzerland’s position as a centre of production and innovation in the long term.
The Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property had changed its practice in March 2026. Since then, the Swiss cross has also been permitted for use with descriptions such as “Swiss Design” or “Swiss Engineering”, even if the product is manufactured entirely abroad. The institute justified the move by stating that the Swiss economy was suffering from the strength of the Swiss franc and high US tariffs.

Law enforcement officers are investigating the possible involvement of former Defense Minister Fedorov’s adviser in the procurement of drones at inflated prices
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:17:15 EEST
23:17:15 KST

Law enforcement officers are investigating the possible involvement of former Defense Minister Fedorov’s adviser in the procurement of drones at inflated prices
Kyiv • UNN
Investigators are examining the involvement of former Defense Minister Giorgi Tskhakaya’s adviser in concluding drone contracts at inflated prices.
The investigation is examining the involvement of former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov’s adviser, Giorgi Tskhakaya, in concluding contracts and inflating drone prices, media expert Oleh Cheslavsky writes, reports UNN.
The media called former Defense Minister Fedorov’s adviser, Giorgi Tskhakaya, “Fedorov’s eyes in the war.” Today, as Oleh Cheslavsky writes, Tskhakaya’s name appears in materials concerning Gurzuf Defense LLC, the manufacturer of Heavy Shot heavy unmanned aerial vehicles.
“According to the available data, the investigation is examining the involvement of former Defense Minister Fedorov’s adviser and Ministry of Defense officials in concluding agreements under which the company received contracts worth more than UAH 4.5 billion during 2023–2025. Let us immediately note: this is the investigation’s version; no one has been publicly notified of suspicion, and all those involved have the right to provide their own explanations,” the media expert reported.
Cheslavsky described the path Gurzuf Defense took from a startup to a recipient of billion-hryvnia state contracts.
“The company for which a charitable foundation raised money through crowdfunding in 2022, because its capacity allowed it to produce ten units a month, turned into a recipient of billion-hryvnia contracts within two years. At the same time, only UAH 84 million has been documented in open procurement records, with the first public contract dated October 2024. The fiftyfold difference traveled through channels that are not visible in the public sphere. According to the available data, the investigation calculated overpricing of more than UAH 900 million, contracts with individual entrepreneurs worth UAH 133 million, some of whose owners are students and pensioners, and transactions with companies showing signs of being fictitious worth another UAH 780 million,” Cheslavsky explained.
The media expert, citing military personnel, claims that Heavy Shot drones are afraid of rain, take a long time to charge, and require a larger crew—that is, extra people under fire.
“The company itself, incidentally, claims exactly the opposite on its website: according to the manufacturer, Heavy Shot drones withstand ‘enemy fire, difficult weather conditions, and intensive loads.’ Somewhere along the way between the website and the frontline, these characteristics are lost, and it is now up to investigators to find out exactly where,” the expert writes.
Power Without a Signature: Who Is Giorgi Tskhakaya
Cheslavsky points out that Tskhakaya worked as an adviser in Ukraine under various institutions, including state bodies, for 10 years “and during that time managed to be an expert on taxes, customs, privatization, subsoil use, urban planning, digital transformation, and, finally, defense procurement.”
“No one person can understand all of this simultaneously,” Cheslavsky believes.
Before moving to Ukraine, Tskhakaya worked in Georgia. There, he held various positions—he was deputy minister of economic development, headed the Revenue Service, and was deputy minister of finance, and later deputy mayor of Tbilisi. After the end of Saakashvili’s presidency, Tskhakaya, along with other members of the former Georgian leader’s team, ended up in Ukraine.
In July 2015, Tskhakaya became a freelance adviser to State Fiscal Service Chairman Roman Nasirov. Tskhakaya was appointed with the stated purpose of providing consulting services “to form an objective public opinion about the activities of the State Fiscal Service.” An adviser for forming public opinion. Cheslavsky points out that the adviser did not have Ukrainian citizenship at the time.
According to Cheslavsky, that same year Tskhakaya introduced the newly appointed head of the Odesa Customs Service, Yuliia Marushevska, to its personnel. What followed was aptly called by the Odesa publication Thesis “the unofficial management of the customs service.” The adviser, who held neither an official position nor citizenship, was given his own office in the building on Haidara Street, which employees dubbed “reception room number two,” next to Marushevska’s “reception room number one.” Everyone who wanted to resolve an issue with customs knew exactly which door to knock on.
"And now about the effectiveness for which it was all undertaken. By an order of the Odesa Regional State Administration in November 2015, a working group was established that was supposed to submit proposals for amendments to the Customs Code to the governor by March 15, 2016. The deadline passed, and no proposals were made public. Instead, as journalists documented, the advisers actively interfered in the customs service’s day-to-day official matters, which the order did not provide for at all," Chieslavsky claims.
The media also contain recollections from the then head of the Odesa regional police, Kostiantyn Shpylovyi, who stated that Tskhakaia was the initiator of the dismantling (without following the proper procedures) of a sign near the Odesa port on Khadzhibei/Bypass Road, which allegedly directed trucks to the port only through the territory of the private company "Euroterminal." Journalists later found out that it was not the road sign in question that had been dismantled at all, and it had to be restored using taxpayers’ money.
"The customs reform ended in roughly the same way: Marushevska left, while the customs service remained the customs service," the media expert notes.
Tskhakaia avoided the fate of the Georgian citizens from Saakashvili’s circle who were expelled from Ukraine in 2017, and by 2020 he was already an adviser at the "Office of Simple Solutions and Results," explaining how Ukraine could quickly carry out privatization worth $10 billion. In 2021, Tskhakaia replaced Saakashvili on the Coordinating Council for Urban Planning. He then appeared on Mykhailo Fedorov’s team at the Ministry of Digital Transformation, now as a digital transformation specialist. And when Fedorov moved to the Ministry of Defense, the adviser moved with him.
"What exactly the adviser does in the defense sector was described in greatest detail by AIN in a profile published in March 2025, and it is a text worth reading slowly. The publication’s sources call Tskhakaia "Fedorov’s eyes on the front": he spends approximately half his time with the troops, gathers information from combat units, and keeps the minister informed. It sounds almost heroic until one remembers that an adviser at the front does not fight but gathers information—and the whole question is what that information subsequently becomes. Two AIN sources call Tskhakaia "one of the ideologues" of the NEXT unit, a structure created by the Ministry of Digital Transformation that tests advanced weapons. Drones of various types pass through NEXT before receiving codification from the Ministry of Defense, and it is through NEXT that Tskhakaia communicates not only with the military but also with manufacturers," Chieslavsky writes.
The media expert points out that during this period large-scale deregulation of the production of drones, electronic warfare systems, ammunition, and other items is taking place. In addition, manufacturers’ margins are growing—from 1% to 25%.
"Deregulation can indeed be an engine of development. The only question is what it becomes when the same people who later meet manufacturers at testing grounds and sit in the offices of the customer write the market rules. The investigation now appears to be calculating the answer to this question—and calculating it in hryvnias," the expert suggests.
Chieslavsky emphasizes that for advisers such as Tskhakaia, the commodity is access to the person who makes decisions. At the same time, the adviser does not undergo a competition or special background check, does not submit declarations, does not sign orders, and does not appear in any document.
"The entire weight of the decision falls on the official who signed it. Meanwhile, the adviser shapes public opinion. Power without a signature: that is the true specialty in which Tskhakaia has, without a doubt, become the best in Ukraine over the past ten years," the author concludes.

In the first half of this year, the plant increased revenue by 7.6% to UAH 38.70 billion but posted a net loss of UAH 1.08 billion, compared with a net profit of UAH 1.64 billion in the first half of last year.
Metinvest is a vertically integrated group of mining and metallurgical enterprises. Syria's state news agency cited the Syrian Foreign Ministry on Sunday as saying Syria and Russia had reached a memorandum of understanding to settle the future of Russian bases at Tartus and Khmeimim.
The bases' future became uncertain after Russian ally Bashar al-Assad fled the country in 2024. The memorandum followed 18 months of intensive negotiations.
The ministry was quoted as saying the Syrian state would take over management of civilian facilities, including Khmeimim airport and the commercial berth at Tartus port, allowing them to gradually integrate into the country's civilian administration.
Military facilities would be repurposed as joint training centers, with the transition to be completed within three months.
Bases help Moscow project power
Russia, which granted asylum to Assad and his family, views the bases as giving it geopolitical clout in the Middle East and as boosting its ability to project power in the region, across the Mediterranean and into Africa.
The Tartus facility is Russia's only Mediterranean repair and replenishment hub, and Moscow has used Syria as a staging post to fly its military contractors in and out of Africa.
"We regard the signing on Aug. 9 of the memorandum between the Russian Federation and the Syrian Arab Republic on the operation of our bases in Khmeimim and Tartus as an important step aimed at further improving bilateral cooperation in the military sphere," the Russian Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
"We believe that reaching this agreement will give further impetus to the development of the full range of relations between our countries, which are based on a long history of friendship and partnership," it added.
A Syrian source familiar with the terms of the deal said Russian forces would still be stationed at the new training centers but did not have details on how many would be there.
A Syrian court sentenced Assad to death on Tuesday after a trial in absentia, convicting him of crimes including killings, torture and arbitrary arrest during the country's nearly 14-year war.
Separately, Russia's state TASS news agency reported that Russia would reopen its cultural center in Damascus — the so-called Russian House — after a Russian delegation held talks with Syrian officials during the weekend.

Ukraine has stopped reporting the number of missiles launched by Russia during attacks — Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has stopped reporting the number of Russian missiles due to security measures. Kyiv needs more interceptors from allies, especially Patriots.
Ukraine has stopped reporting the number of missiles launched by Russia during attacks, while continuing to appeal to its allies for help strengthening its air defense, UNN reports, citing Bloomberg.
Details
The publication notes that although the Air Defense Forces said that 98 of 120 Russian drones had been shot down overnight, they did not provide data on the number of missiles launched. This came several days after they stopped reporting the interception of ballistic missiles following last week’s attack, during which Ukraine failed to stop any of the 28 projectiles.
According to a source familiar with the situation, who wished to remain anonymous because of the sensitivity of the matter, the Air Defense Forces changed the reporting format as a security measure in response to Russian strikes.
The media outlet notes that Ukraine is making every effort to obtain more interceptors from its allies, as it has struggled to counter the Russian air attacks that have intensified in recent weeks. In particular, it needs additional deliveries for the U.S.-made Patriot system, the most effective system for destroying Russian ballistic missiles, amid a sharp rise in global demand caused by the conflict in the Middle East.
A hospital building and businesses were damaged in a missile strike in Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday on the X platform. According to him, the city of Zaporizhzhia was hit by North Korean-made ballistic missiles, as well as Russian Zircon hypersonic cruise missiles.
Deliveries of anti-aircraft missiles to Ukraine from its allies fell threefold in the first half of the year compared with 2025, Zelenskyy said on August 5, after Russian strikes that Kyiv’s forces were unable to repel killed at least 17 people and injured dozens.
According to the Ministry of Defense, Ukraine intercepted 29 of the 195 Russian ballistic missiles launched in July, while another 40 failed to reach their targets.
Additionally
Bloomberg noted that Ukraine is responding by striking oil refineries and logistics warehouses deep inside Russia, including warehouses belonging to e-commerce giant Wildberries, as part of a campaign aimed at causing economic damage and bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians.
"As of August 2026, more than 300 long-range drones are flying against us every night," Iryna Terekh, CEO of Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point, said on X on Tuesday. "Since the beginning of the year, Ukraine has carried out twice as many deep strikes" against Russia as Moscow’s forces have against Ukraine, she added.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense reported that its forces intercepted 396 Ukrainian drones overnight in 14 regions of the country and in Crimea. Russia annexed Ukraine’s Black Sea peninsula in 2014.
Drone strikes caused fires at two warehouses in the southern Voronezh region overnight, the region’s governor, Alexander Gusev, said on Telegram. Wildberries’ press service later said that the fires had been extinguished and that most of the goods were not damaged.
"Russian forces are redirecting production of their long-range strike systems toward those that can more reliably penetrate Ukrainian air defenses," the U.S.-based Institute for the Study of War said in an assessment published on X on Tuesday. "The Kremlin believes it can exploit Ukraine’s shortage of missile interceptors to avoid the need to engage in meaningful negotiations or make concessions on its maximalist demands."
As a reminder
As UNN reported, Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with 120 drones, striking Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia with ballistic and Zircon missiles; 98 drones were shot down or suppressed, Ukraine’s Air Force said on Tuesday, without specifying the number of missiles launched by Russia.

"Did I Really Approve This?": What Happens Behind the Scenes of Online Course Production
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:01:39 EEST
23:01:39 KST

Great online courses are a bit like great books for self-education. They broaden your perspective, make you think, and provide practical knowledge you can actually use in everyday life. At Zrozumilo!, we keep things concise: up to ten lectures, each around ten minutes long, plus quizzes and interactive activities.
At first glance, it might seem like there is not much to it. After all, the final product is only about 100 minutes of video content. But behind those 100 minutes are at least three months of work from concept to launch, along with anywhere from five to twenty (often exhausting) hours spent filming in the studio. And no matter how many courses you have produced, the chances that something will go wrong on shoot day are always close to 100%.
Technical mishaps are usually the easiest to anticipate. If a problem cannot be fixed with duct tape, you probably just need more duct tape. (Extra batteries and memory cards are absolute essentials, too.) Of course, working in Ukraine comes with its own unique challenges. Mass attacks and power outages are impossible to predict. Whether the studio remains intact, whether there is a stable connection, or whether air raid sirens interrupt the recording often comes down to sheer luck.
But the biggest challenge of all is usually the human factor.
Risk #1: The Teleprompter Effect, or "Did I Really Approve This?"
"Did I Really Approve This?" is the phrase every project manager and crew member hears dozens of times during a filming day.
The irony is that in 95% of cases, the very person asking the question is the one who wrote, reviewed, and personally approved the script they are now struggling to read on camera.
But a new role, bright studio lights, nerves, and plain old fatigue can work wonders. Even experienced professionals start running out of steam by the fifth lecture, and that is completely normal. Comments like these are often just a natural reaction to a stressful situation.
Behind-the-scenes tip: Be prepared for this emotionally. Speakers need encouragement, short breaks, and reassurance that they are not expected to perform like professional TV presenters from the very first take.
Risk #2: The “I Look Better Without Glasses” Syndrome
Sometimes preparing for a shoot feels like detective work.
For three months, you are in constant communication with a speaker who assures you they are completely comfortable on camera and have plenty of on-screen experience. Then the camera starts rolling, and suddenly they become self-conscious and struggle to deliver a lecture confidently.
Or there is the classic scenario: on the day of filming, a person who has worn glasses their entire life decides they would look better on camera without them and leaves them at home.
How are they supposed to read from the teleprompter now? Good question.
Behind-the-scenes tip: Schedule a rehearsal in front of a camera, or at least over Zoom. Discuss even the smallest details in advance. Remind speakers about glasses, contact lenses, camera angles, and wardrobe choices long before filming begins.
Risk #3: The Treacherous Bar Stool and Other Small Details
Ergonomics is one of those things people often overlook until it is too late.
For example, you decide to create a more stylish set and bring in a tall bar stool. What you fail to consider is that your speaker happens to be rather short. The result? An awkward look on camera, numb legs, and a day-long struggle for the person expected to sit there for hours.
Behind-the-scenes tip: A beautiful shot matters, but so does the speaker's comfort. Take care of that, and you may even avoid the first risk entirely.
In Conclusion: Every Effortless Lecture Is the Result of Complex Project Management
When viewers press play on a ten-minute video lecture on Zrozumilo!, they see polished visuals, a confident expert, and a clear structure. And that is exactly how a high-quality educational product should work. Viewers should never have to think about how the content was created.
What they do not see is the invisible, meticulous, and often stressful work happening behind the scenes. The work of project managers who, at any given moment, must also become directors, psychologists, and crisis managers. The people who can find the right camera angle in seconds, calm a nervous speaker, restore their confidence, gently joke about the “mysterious scriptwriter,” and, if necessary, pull out yet another roll of duct tape.
Producing online courses is not just about recording videos. It is about managing expectations, emotions, and unpredictable circumstances. And ultimately, it is the ability to adapt when everything goes off script that turns a team into true professionals and transforms a course into something not only successful, but genuinely valuable for its audience.

Over UAH 16 million in combat payments without participating in battles — a serviceman in Lviv region has been served with a notice of suspicion
Kyiv • UNN
A military official in Lviv region signed orders to pay UAH 100,000 to servicemen who did not participate in battles. UAH 16 million was unjustifiably paid from the budget; he faces up to 8 years in prison.
Law enforcement officers notified a military official, who was temporarily serving as the commander of one of the military units in the Lviv region, of suspicion. The officer was charged with negligent treatment of military service under martial law, which resulted in more than UAH 16 million in additional combat participation payments being unjustifiably paid from the state budget. This was reported by UNN, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Details
The investigation established that the official was responsible for organizing service in the military unit, keeping personnel records, and was supposed to have information about which service members were directly involved in combat operations and the performance of combat missions.
Between February and March 2024, he signed orders authorizing increased additional remuneration of UAH 100,000 per month, which included service members who, according to the investigation, did not directly participate in combat operations, did not ensure the implementation of national security and defense measures, and did not perform combat missions that would have entitled them to such payments.
A total of UAH 16,081,000 was paid from the state budget without proper legal grounds.
The individual involved was notified of suspicion under Part 4 of Article 425 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine—negligent treatment of service by a military official, which caused grave consequences and was committed under martial law.
The article provides for punishment in the form of imprisonment for a term of 5 to 8 years.
It will be recalled
In cases involving procurement for the military, payments to service members, corruption during mobilization, and illegal transportation across the border, 488 individuals have been notified of suspicion in 384 criminal proceedings, while 530 indictments have already been sent to court.

The monument from the grave of Yevhen Konovalets, Colonel of the Army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic (UNR) and first head of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), in Rotterdam (Netherlands) will be brought to Ukraine as a memorial object, and the burial site itself will be memorialized, reported Head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINP) Oleksandr Alforov.

Yevhen Konovalets (1891–1938) was a prominent Ukrainian military and political figure, Colonel of the UNR Army, Commander of the Sich Riflemen Corps, founder of the Ukrainian Military Organization (UVO), and the first Head of the Leadership of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN).
Konovalets was assassinated on May 23, 1938, by Soviet foreign intelligence agent Pavel Sudoplatov, and buried at the Crooswijk cemetery in Rotterdam, Netherlands.
As reported, on August 11, a ceremony for the exhumation of the remains of prominent Ukrainian military and political figure Colonel Yevhen Konovalets took place in Rotterdam (Netherlands). His ashes will be returned to Ukraine and reburied at the National Military Memorial Cemetery (NVMC). The farewell ceremony will take place at the Patriarchal Cathedral of the Resurrection of Christ of the UGCC in Kyiv.

Somalia: Survey of displaced families in Baidoa finds every second child malnourished
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
13:47:31 UTC
22:47:31 KST

- An MSF survey has found shocking levels of malnutrition among children in displacement sites in Baidoa, Somalia.
- Malnutrition and displacement are most severely affecting women and children across the country, as donors continue to withdraw their support.
- MSF calls on the donor community to ensure an adequately funded emergency response in Baidoa and other affected areas.
Baidoa / Nairobi — One in every two children screened in displacement sites in Baidoa, South-West state, Somalia, is acutely malnourished and one in every four is severely malnourished. These shocking statistics are the findings of a malnutrition survey carried out in July by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF).
“Behind every statistic is a child,” says Allara Ali, MSF's project coordinator in Somalia. “What we are seeing is shocking and far beyond the threshold of an extremely critical emergency.”
“What is equally shocking is the lack of urgency from donors who continue to downscale and withdraw support from Somalia,” says Ali. “While other organisations are attempting to respond, their capacity is limited by funding constraints.”
The results are consistent with MSF’s regular malnutrition surveillance in Baidoa, where teams have screened more than 21,000 children under five since the beginning of the year and found global acute malnutrition levels of around 50 per cent.
The survey, conducted across 888 households in 14 displacement sites in Baidoa, also found that one-third of families are surviving on just one meal a day, while only two per cent can afford three meals a day.
MSF is urgently calling on the donor community, international organisations, and health authorities to ensure a well-coordinated, adequately funded and effective emergency response without delay in Baidoa and other affected areas of Somalia.
“The world cannot wait for a famine declaration before acting,” says Ali. “Action is needed now to prevent loss of lives.”
Consecutive failed rains and worsening drought have affected hundreds of thousands of people across Somalia, depriving families of food, water, crops and livestock. According to the UN, in the first three months of 2026, more than half a million people were displaced in Somalia, with nine out of 10 displacements driven by drought. Alarmingly, 85 per cent of those displaced are women and children, who are also among the most severely affected by malnutrition.

Since the beginning of the year, more than 21,000 children have been admitted to MSF-supported outpatient malnutrition facilities in Baidoa — more than double the number recorded during the same period last year. Over the same period, 2,890 children have been admitted for inpatient care, an increase of 78 per cent compared with the same period in 2025. Figures in 2025 were already higher than the year before. A similar trend is being seen in Mudug, where admissions to MSF-supported inpatient facilities increased by 70 per cent in June and July.
“It is rare that we are able to get two meals a day,” says Nuriyo, mother of a child being treated for severe acute malnutrition in Baidoa. “There is no organisation helping us. An organisation gave us some cash assistance, but that was three years ago.”
Measles and diphtheria are spreading in a context where vaccination campaigns are not reaching everyone effectively. Since the beginning of the year, MSF has treated around 2,500 measles cases in Baidoa, compared with about 1,700 cases during all of 2025. Pregnant and lactating women are also severely affected. In the past two months alone, MSF has admitted more than 2,600 pregnant and breastfeeding women for malnutrition support. When mothers are malnourished, the risks extend to their babies — before birth, during delivery, and in the first months of life.
To respond to the surge in patients, MSF has expanded one medical facility from 50 to 150 beds. MSF teams have also distributed relief items to displaced families and are trucking safe water to displaced communities in Mudug and Baidoa. But medical care and emergency assistance alone cannot meet the scale of this crisis.
“A hospital bed can save a child today. But it cannot protect that child if they return to a shelter with no food, no clean water and no basic services,” says Ali. “Without comprehensive support, including social protection, the cycle of relapse and readmission will continue.”
Despite the level of suffering, Somalia is being deprioritised by major donors, including the United Kingdom and the United States. Somalia’s humanitarian response plan has been reduced by 40 per cent in 2026 and was still less than one-third funded by July. Funding cuts are weakening already fragile health services and forcing the health system to absorb a crisis far beyond its capacity.
“The malnutrition and health crisis in South-West [state], Somalia, is becoming a clear example of dangerous indifference and a failure of responsibility, as Somalia is pushed further down the global agenda,” says Ali. “The scale of this crisis should be a wake-up call for the international community.”
MSF is calling for an urgent scale-up of inpatient treatment for severe acute malnutrition, particularly for children with medical complications. This must include increased bed capacity and additional medical staff, as well as uninterrupted supplies of therapeutic food, medicines and medical equipment. We also urge vaccination campaigns to reach missed and hard-to-reach communities, with stronger coverage and more effective delivery.
According to the latest IPC analysis, around six million people in Somalia – about one in three people – are estimated to be facing food shortages. Among them, nearly 1.9 million people are in an emergency, meaning they need urgent support.
Nearly 512,000 people were newly displaced within Somalia during the first three months of 2026 alone, with 93 per cent displaced by drought. About 85 per cent of people who are displaced are women and children (UNHCR June 2026).
Somalia’s Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan was reduced to US$852 million in 2026. Humanitarian partners target 2.4 million people, reaching less than half of those in need.
International organisation CARE says funding shortfalls have forced the closure of 50 of its 80 supported health and nutrition centres in Somalia since January, with 15 more at risk by October.
United States, one of Somalia’s leading donors for years, including in 2025, has fully halted its support in 2026, while the United Kingdom has cut its funding by nearly half compared with 2025. (UNOCHA).
As per IPC, Somalia faced a similarly severe malnutrition crisis as in 2022, with nearly 1.88 million children expected to need treatment in 2026 — but international support has fallen by 88 per cent compared with 2022.
